title: Admiral Car Insurance Review
meta_title: Admiral Car Insurance Review 2026: MultiCar and Cover
meta_description: Admiral's comprehensive cover is 5-star Defaqto rated. What MultiCar saves, what each tier includes, and the two things to check before you buy.
intro:
Admiral's comprehensive car insurance carries a 5-star Defaqto rating, the top mark an independent assessor gives, and the range runs from Platinum down through Gold and Admiral. Windscreen cover, a courtesy car at approved garages and child car seat cover come as standard on the comprehensive tiers, and Platinum folds in European cover and roadside breakdown so there is nothing left to bolt on.

MultiCar is the reason most households end up here. Insure two or three vehicles on a single policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus, and the combined price is usually below the sum of separate policies. It bites hardest for parents insuring a young driver alongside their own cars, where premiums in isolation are punishing. There is a MultiCover equivalent for bundling car and home.

The excess options are unusually granular too — £50 steps from £0 to £500, then £700, £750 and £1,000 — which gives real control over the premium. Two things to read before buying: the cut-price Essential tier is a different product from the rest of the range, and the admin fees are worth pricing in. Both are covered below.

sections.heading: MultiCar: the actual reason to choose Admiral
sections.html:
MultiCar lets a household insure several vehicles under one policy, each with its own no-claims bonus, at a combined price usually below the sum of separate policies.

It suits a specific household shape: two working adults with a car each, or parents insuring a young driver alongside their own vehicles. The second case is where it bites hardest, because young-driver premiums are punishing in isolation and the MultiCar structure softens that considerably.

MultiCover extends the same idea to home insurance, bundling car and home for a further discount.

One thing to check rather than assume: the vehicles generally need to be at the same address. Adding a car kept at a student address or a second home is where MultiCar quotes tend to fall over, and it is worth confirming before you build a renewal plan around it.

If you are a single-car household with no home insurance to bundle, the main argument for Admiral disappears and you should be comparing purely on price and cover level.

sections.heading: Where the cover is genuinely good
sections.html:
Set Essential aside and the rest of the range is strong.

Platinum bundles European cover, windscreen, courtesy car and roadside breakdown into one policy, which removes the add-on juggling that makes comparison sites so misleading. Gold is the same shape with breakdown optional.

The voluntary excess range is unusually granular — £50 increments from £0 to £500, then £700, £750 and £1,000. Most insurers offer four or five options. That granularity lets you tune the premium precisely rather than jumping between wide bands.

Child car seat cover as standard across all comprehensive tiers is a small but genuine inclusion; seats must be replaced after any impact and they are not cheap.

Courtesy cars come through Admiral-approved garages, which is standard practice but does mean you use their repair network rather than your own choice of garage.

sections.heading: Essential is not a cheaper version of the same policy
sections.html:
It is a materially different product, and the two omissions matter.

No windscreen cover. A replacement windscreen on a modern car with camera-based driver assistance frequently runs past £500 once recalibration is included. On every other Admiral comprehensive tier that is covered. On Essential you pay it.

No European cover. Drive to France on an Essential policy and you are running on the legal minimum required in that country, not comprehensive cover. Damage to your own vehicle is not covered.

The Defaqto exclusion is the clearest signal available. Admiral's comprehensive range is 5-star rated and Essential specifically is not included in that rating — an independent assessor declining to put it in the same category as its siblings.

Essential makes sense for an older, low-value car that never leaves the UK, where you have decided a cracked windscreen is a cost you would absorb anyway. For anything else the saving is smaller than the exposure.

sections.heading: The admin fees deserve attention
sections.html:
Around £15 to amend a policy, and £60 to £160 to cancel, depending on circumstances.

The cancellation range is the one to note. If you sell a car mid-term, write it off, or simply find a better price at month seven, you are paying a fee that can approach the cost of two months' premium. That materially changes the maths on switching mid-policy.

Amendment fees add up too if your circumstances move — a change of address, a change of job title, adding a named driver. None are large individually, but a policy that gets amended three times has quietly cost £45 more than the quoted premium.

Compare that against insurers offering free amendments if you expect your details to change during the year.

pros: MultiCar discount is the strongest reason to choose Admiral for a multi-vehicle household
MultiCover extends the discount to bundled car and home insurance
5-star Defaqto rating on the comprehensive range (Essential excluded)
Platinum bundles European cover, windscreen, courtesy car and breakdown in one policy
Unusually granular voluntary excess options, £0 to £1,000
Child car seat cover included on all comprehensive tiers
Courtesy car included with comprehensive cover
cons: Essential tier has no windscreen cover and no European cover, and is excluded from the Defaqto rating
Cancellation fees of £60 to £160 make mid-term switching expensive
£15 amendment fee for policy changes adds up over a year
Courtesy car requires using Admiral-approved garages rather than your own
MultiCar generally requires vehicles at the same address
Single-car households without home insurance lose the main advantage
verdict: Strong if you have more than one vehicle, or a car and home policy to bundle — MultiCar and MultiCover are genuinely competitive and hard to beat by shopping separately. Take Platinum or Gold rather than Essential: the missing windscreen and European cover are worth more than the saving, and Defaqto's refusal to include Essential in the 5-star rating tells you what an independent assessor makes of it. If you are a single-car household with no bundle to build, compare on price like any other insurer, and factor the £60–£160 cancellation fee into any plan to switch mid-term.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Admiral and Admiral Essential?
faqs.a: Essential removes windscreen cover and European cover, and is excluded from Admiral's 5-star Defaqto rating. The standard Admiral, Gold and Platinum tiers include windscreen cover and carry the rating.

faqs.q: How does MultiCar work?
faqs.a: You insure several vehicles under one policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus, at a combined price usually lower than separate policies. Vehicles generally need to be at the same address — confirm this before relying on it.

faqs.q: What are Admiral's admin fees?
faqs.a: Roughly £15 to amend a policy and £60 to £160 to cancel, depending on circumstances. The cancellation fee is worth factoring in if you might switch mid-term or sell the car.

faqs.q: Is a courtesy car included?
faqs.a: Yes with comprehensive cover, provided the repair goes through an Admiral-approved garage. Using your own choice of garage may forfeit it.

faqs.q: Does Admiral cover driving in Europe?
faqs.a: Platinum includes European cover. Essential excludes it entirely, leaving you on the legal minimum abroad rather than comprehensive cover.

title: Admiral Home Insurance Review: Buildings and Contents Cover
meta_title: Admiral Buildings and Contents Insurance Review 2026
meta_description: Admiral home and contents insurance compared across all three tiers. Contents limits, the £2,000 single-item rule, and what MultiCover saves.
intro:
Admiral sells buildings and contents insurance across three tiers — Admiral, Gold and Platinum — and the differences between them are more specific than the names suggest.

Buildings cover is unlimited rebuild cost on all three, which removes the single biggest risk in home insurance: under-insuring the structure. Where they diverge is contents, which runs £100,000 on Admiral, £125,000 on Gold and £150,000 on Platinum, and in what comes included rather than as a paid extra.

The clause that catches most people is the same at every tier: any single item worth more than £2,000 must be specified individually or it is not covered for its full value. That applies to an engagement ring, a road bike, a laptop, a watch. It is the most common reason a contents claim pays out less than the owner expected.

sections.heading: Which tier, decided by what is included rather than the headline
sections.html:
The contents limits — £100,000, £125,000, £150,000 — are a distraction for most households. Very few people have £100,000 of contents, so that ceiling rarely binds.

What actually separates the tiers is what stops being an add-on:

  • Admiral — accidental damage, home emergency and legal cover are all optional extras.
  • Gold — audiovisual accidental damage and home emergency (£500) are included. Full contents accidental damage and legal remain optional.
  • Platinum — everything is included: full accidental damage, home emergency at £1,000, and legal cover up to £100,000.

Price the add-ons individually before assuming the base tier is cheaper. Buying Admiral plus accidental damage plus home emergency plus legal frequently costs more than Platinum with all four built in, and leaves you with a lower home emergency limit.

Accidental damage is the add-on worth having if you have children, pets or hard flooring. It covers the spilled paint, the foot through the ceiling, the television knocked off its stand — none of which are covered by standard contents cover.

sections.heading: Unlimited rebuild cost removes the classic mistake
sections.html:
Under-insurance on buildings is the most expensive error in home insurance, and it is easy to make. Rebuild cost is not market value — it is what it would cost to demolish and reconstruct the property, and on older or unusual houses it can exceed what the house would sell for.

Get that figure too low and insurers apply average: insure for half the true rebuild cost and a £20,000 claim pays £10,000, even though £20,000 is well within your sum insured.

Admiral offers unlimited rebuild cost cover on all three tiers, which sidesteps the problem entirely. You are not asked to estimate a figure you have no way of calculating accurately.

For a period property, a thatched roof, a converted barn or anything non-standard, that is worth more than a small premium difference elsewhere.

sections.heading: The £2,000 rule is the one to act on
sections.html:
Contents cover pays out per item as well as in total. Admiral's unspecified single-item limit is £2,000 across all tiers. Anything worth more must be listed by name on the policy.

What that catches in an ordinary house:

  • An engagement or wedding ring — frequently over £2,000 on its own
  • A road or e-bike — £3,000 is unremarkable now
  • A camera body plus lenses, if claimed as one item
  • A watch, a laptop, a musical instrument

Claim for a stolen £4,500 ring that was never specified and you receive £2,000. The shortfall is not a technicality — it is what the policy says.

Do this before you buy, not at renewal: walk through the house and list anything worth more than £2,000, then declare each one. It usually adds little to the premium and it is the difference between being insured and being partly insured.

sections.heading: MultiCover, and the fees to price in
sections.html:
MultiCover discounts home insurance when you also hold Admiral car cover. If your car is already with Admiral, get the home quote before shopping elsewhere — the bundled price is often below what a standalone home policy costs.

The reverse holds too: if you are buying home insurance here and your car renews soon, price the pair together rather than separately.

Two fees to factor in. Around £15 to amend a policy, and £60 to £160 to cancel. Home policies get amended more than people expect — adding a specified item, a change after building work, a new occupant — and those £15s accumulate. The cancellation fee matters if you move house mid-term, which is common enough to price in rather than ignore.

pros: Unlimited rebuild cost on buildings across all three tiers, removing under-insurance risk
Platinum bundles full accidental damage, £1,000 home emergency and legal cover as standard
MultiCover discount when bundled with Admiral car insurance
Contents limits up to £150,000 on Platinum
Clear three-tier structure rather than a confusing add-on maze
Gold includes audiovisual accidental damage and home emergency as standard
cons: £2,000 single-item limit means valuables must be specified individually or are underpaid
Base Admiral tier makes accidental damage, home emergency and legal all paid extras
Home emergency capped at £500 on Admiral and Gold, half the Platinum limit
£60–£160 cancellation fee stings if you move house mid-term
£15 amendment fee adds up when specifying items or changing details
Contents ceilings are largely irrelevant to most households, which makes tier comparison harder than it looks
verdict: Strong on the thing that matters most — unlimited rebuild cost on buildings at every tier means you cannot under-insure the structure, which is the costliest mistake in home insurance. Compare Platinum against the base tier with add-ons bolted on before deciding; Platinum frequently wins on price and always wins on the home emergency limit. Whichever tier you take, list every item worth over £2,000 before the policy starts. If your car is already with Admiral, get the MultiCover quote first.

faqs.q: Does Admiral cover buildings and contents together?
faqs.a: Yes. You can buy buildings and contents as a combined policy across all three tiers. Buildings cover is unlimited rebuild cost; contents is capped at £100,000, £125,000 or £150,000 depending on tier.

faqs.q: What is the single-item limit?
faqs.a: £2,000. Anything worth more must be specified individually on the policy or it will only be covered up to £2,000. This catches engagement rings, bikes, watches and cameras most often.

faqs.q: Is accidental damage included?
faqs.a: Only on Platinum for full contents. Gold includes accidental damage for audiovisual equipment. On the base Admiral tier it is an optional extra for both.

faqs.q: What does unlimited rebuild cost mean?
faqs.a: You are not asked to estimate what it would cost to rebuild your home, so you cannot under-insure it. Under-insuring buildings triggers 'average', where claims are scaled down in proportion to the shortfall.

faqs.q: How much is home emergency cover?
faqs.a: £500 on the Admiral tier as an optional extra, £500 included on Gold, and £1,000 included on Platinum.

title: Admiral Motorbike Insurance Review
meta_title: Admiral Motorbike Insurance Review 2026: Multi-Bike and Cover
meta_description: Admiral motorbike insurance reviewed: multi-bike discounts, helmet and leathers cover, European use, and what the tiers actually include.
intro:
Motorbike insurance is priced on a different logic to car insurance, and the gap between a good policy and a cheap one shows up in three places: what happens to your gear, whether you can ride in Europe, and how many bikes you can put on one policy.

Admiral covers scooters, commuters, cruisers and sports bikes, with multi-bike discounts for riders who own more than one. Cover runs from third party through to comprehensive, with optional breakdown, helmet and leathers protection, and legal expenses.

The thing most riders get wrong is assuming their kit is covered. A helmet, jacket, boots and gloves easily represent £1,200 of equipment, and standard comprehensive cover does not automatically replace them after a crash.

sections.heading: Multi-bike: the main reason to be here
sections.html:
Riders who own more than one machine — a commuter and a weekend bike, a project in the garage, a classic — usually pay considerably more insuring them separately than together.

Admiral's multi-bike arrangement puts several machines on one policy with a combined discount and a single renewal date. If you own two or more bikes, this is the first quote to get.

It also works alongside MultiCar, so a bike can sit on the same household policy as cars — useful for a rider whose partner drives, or a household with a van and a bike.

Two things to confirm rather than assume: that the machines are kept at the same address, and how a claim on one affects the no-claims bonus on the others. Policies vary on the second point and it matters more than the discount.

sections.heading: Storage and security: declare it accurately
sections.html:
Motorcycle theft is concentrated and opportunistic, and insurers price it hard. Where the bike is kept overnight — locked garage, driveway, on the street — moves the premium substantially, and so do declared security measures like a ground anchor, chain, disc lock, tracker or alarm.

Declaring a garage you do not use, or security you have not fitted, is the fastest way to have a theft claim declined. Insurers investigate theft claims closely because the fraud rate is high, and the security question is the first thing they check.

Conversely, if you have fitted a Thatcham-approved immobiliser or tracker and not told them, you are paying more than you need to. Re-declare after any security upgrade.

sections.heading: Your gear is not covered by default
sections.html:
Add it up honestly. A decent helmet is £300 to £600. A textile or leather jacket, £200 to £500. Boots, gloves, trousers — another £300. Most riders are wearing £1,000 to £1,500 of equipment before the bike is considered.

Standard comprehensive cover insures the motorcycle. Riding gear is normally a separate add-on, and when you buy it there are two things to check:

  • The limit. Some policies cap gear cover at £500, which does not replace a helmet and a jacket together.
  • Whether the helmet is covered after any impact. A helmet that has been dropped or crashed in must be replaced whether or not it looks damaged — the protective structure is single-use. A policy that only pays for visible damage misses the point.

This add-on is usually cheap relative to what it covers, and it is the one most worth taking.

sections.heading: European riding and the tour trap
sections.html:
If you ride abroad, check the European allowance rather than assuming comprehensive cover follows you.

Many policies include a limited number of days of European use, and drop to third-party-only beyond it. A rider on a two-week Alpine tour can find that days eleven to fourteen are uninsured for damage to their own bike — the point at which the roads get most interesting.

Where the allowance is short, extending it for the trip is usually inexpensive. The mistake is discovering the limit after the trip rather than before.

Breakdown cover deserves the same treatment. Recovery of a motorcycle from mainland Europe is expensive and specialist, and standard UK breakdown cover generally does not extend to it.

pros: Multi-bike discount for riders with more than one machine on a single policy
Works alongside MultiCar, so a bike can sit with household cars
Full range from third party through to comprehensive
Covers scooters through to sports bikes rather than a narrow band
Helmet, leathers, breakdown and legal cover all available as add-ons
Single renewal date across multiple machines
cons: Riding gear is an add-on, not standard — and default limits may not replace a helmet and jacket
European cover is day-limited; exceeding it can drop you to third party abroad
£60–£160 cancellation fee, which bites if you sell the bike mid-season
Multi-bike generally requires machines at the same address
Declared security and storage must be accurate or a theft claim can be refused
UK breakdown cover does not usually extend to European recovery
verdict: The strongest case for Admiral is multi-bike — if you own two or more machines, or a bike alongside household cars, the combined price is hard to beat by shopping separately. Whichever insurer you end up with, take the helmet and leathers add-on and check its limit against what you actually wear, because £1,200 of gear is not covered by a standard comprehensive policy. If you tour, confirm the European day allowance before booking rather than after, and be scrupulously accurate about where the bike is kept overnight.

faqs.q: Is my helmet and riding gear covered?
faqs.a: Not as standard. Helmet and leathers cover is normally an optional add-on. Check the limit — some cap at £500, which will not replace a helmet and jacket together — and confirm the helmet is replaced after any impact rather than only when visibly damaged.

faqs.q: Can I insure more than one bike?
faqs.a: Yes. Admiral's multi-bike arrangement covers several machines on one policy with a combined discount and one renewal date. Bikes generally need to be at the same address. Ask how a claim on one affects the no-claims bonus on the others.

faqs.q: Am I covered riding in Europe?
faqs.a: European cover is available but usually limited to a set number of days. Beyond the allowance you may drop to third-party-only. Check the limit before a long tour and extend it if needed.

faqs.q: How does where I keep the bike affect the price?
faqs.a: Substantially. A locked garage prices very differently to street parking, and declared security like a ground anchor, chain, tracker or alarm reduces the premium. Declare it accurately — theft claims are investigated closely and this is the first thing checked.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: Between £60 and £160 depending on circumstances, plus around £15 for amendments. Worth factoring in if you might sell the bike at the end of the season.

title: Admiral Van Insurance Review
meta_title: Admiral Van Insurance Review 2026: Cover, Tools and MultiCar
meta_description: Admiral van insurance and where it fits. Social versus commercial use, tools cover, MultiCar with your car, and the fees to know about.
intro:
Van insurance turns on one question that car insurance never asks: what is the van actually for?

Social-only, carriage of own goods, and hire-and-reward are three different products at three very different prices, and declaring the wrong one is the most common reason a van claim gets refused. A tradesman who insures for social use because it was cheaper has effectively bought nothing.

Admiral's van proposition is built on the same foundations as its car cover — MultiCar, MultiCover, tiered comprehensive policies — but the use-class question sits in front of all of it, and it deserves more attention than the premium does.

sections.heading: Get the use class right or nothing else matters
sections.html:
Three classes, and the gap between them is the whole ballgame:

  • Social, domestic and pleasure — the van is personal transport. Cheapest, and useless to anyone working from it.
  • Carriage of own goods — you carry your own tools, stock or equipment for your own business. This is what most tradespeople need.
  • Hire and reward — you carry goods belonging to other people for payment. Couriers, deliveries, man-and-van work.

Insurers check use class when a claim is made, not when the premium is taken. A plumber insured social-only who crashes on the way to a job can find the claim declined and the policy voided — which then has to be declared on every future application.

The saving from under-declaring is typically modest. The consequence is total. If you use the van for work in any capacity, buy the class that reflects it.

sections.heading: Where MultiCar changes the calculation
sections.html:
Admiral's MultiCar scheme lets a van sit on the same policy as household cars, each keeping its own no-claims bonus.

This is genuinely useful for a sole trader with a work van and a family car, or a small operation running two vans and a car. The combined price is usually below the sum of separate policies, and there is one renewal date instead of three.

MultiCover adds home insurance to the bundle for a further discount — relevant if you are self-employed and working from home anyway.

The same caveat applies as with cars: vehicles generally need to be at the same address. A van kept at a yard or lock-up rather than your home may not qualify, and that is worth confirming before building a renewal strategy around it.

sections.heading: Tools are usually not covered, and that surprises people
sections.html:
Van insurance covers the van. It does not automatically cover what is inside it.

Tools cover is generally an add-on, and when you buy it there are three things to check rather than assume:

  • The limit. A working tradesman's van can hold £5,000 to £15,000 of equipment. Add-on limits are often far lower.
  • Overnight conditions. Many policies exclude theft from a van left on the street overnight, or require tools to be removed entirely between certain hours. This is the clause that defeats most tools claims.
  • Whether individual high-value items need listing. A £900 laser level may need naming specifically to be covered.

If tools are your livelihood, read this section of the policy wording before comparing premiums. A cheaper policy with a £1,000 tools limit and an overnight exclusion is not cheaper in any meaningful sense.

sections.heading: Two things to confirm before buying
sections.html:
Does the courtesy vehicle come as a van? A courtesy car is worthless to someone whose van is their working vehicle. Some policies provide a like-for-like van, some provide a small car, and some provide nothing on van policies at all. If your income depends on the vehicle, this is the most important line in the policy.

What are the cancellation terms? Admiral's fees run to £60–£160 to cancel and around £15 to amend. Vans change hands more often than cars — upgrading as a business grows, or downsizing when work is thin — so mid-term cancellation is a realistic scenario rather than a hypothetical one.

pros: MultiCar allows a van and household cars on one policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus
MultiCover extends the discount to home insurance, useful for home-based sole traders
One renewal date instead of several across vehicles
Wide voluntary excess range for tuning the premium
Established insurer with 24/7 claims support
cons: Tools cover is generally an add-on rather than standard, with limits and overnight exclusions to check
Courtesy vehicle may not be a like-for-like van — confirm before buying
Cancellation fees of £60 to £160 matter more for vans, which change hands often
MultiCar generally requires vehicles at the same address, which rules out yard-kept vans
Use class must be declared accurately or a claim can be refused and the policy voided
verdict: Worth a quote if you have other vehicles to bundle — MultiCar is the strongest part of Admiral's proposition and a van sits in it naturally alongside a family car. Before comparing premiums, settle two things: declare the correct use class, because under-declaring voids the policy at the worst possible moment, and check whether tools cover and a like-for-like courtesy van are included or extra. For a working van those two clauses matter more than the price difference between insurers.

faqs.q: What use class do I need?
faqs.a: Social only if the van is purely personal transport. Carriage of own goods if you carry your own tools or stock for your business — this covers most tradespeople. Hire and reward if you carry other people's goods for payment. Declaring the wrong class can void the policy.

faqs.q: Are my tools covered?
faqs.a: Not usually as standard. Tools cover is generally an add-on. Check the limit, whether high-value items must be listed individually, and any overnight conditions — many policies exclude theft from a van left on the street overnight.

faqs.q: Will I get a courtesy van?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Some policies provide a like-for-like van, some a small car, some nothing at all on van cover. Confirm this specifically if the van is how you earn.

faqs.q: Can I put my van on a MultiCar policy?
faqs.a: Yes. Vans can sit alongside cars on one Admiral policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus. Vehicles generally need to be at the same address, so a van kept at a separate yard may not qualify.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: Between £60 and £160 depending on circumstances, plus around £15 for amendments. Worth factoring in if you change vans regularly.

title: Aviva Car Insurance
meta_title: Aviva Car Insurance Review: Limits, Excesses and Extras
meta_description: Aviva’s comprehensive limits, the £10 and £115 glass excesses, EV charging cover and its own complaints figures. Checked August 2026.
intro:
Aviva writes its motor policies through Aviva Insurance Limited, a company registered in Scotland at Pitheavlis in Perth under number SC002116, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the PRA and the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 202153. That reference is worth keeping: it lets you confirm on the Financial Services Register that the company taking your premium is the company carrying the risk, which is not always the case with motor brands sold online.

Scale is the first thing a driver is buying here. Aviva served almost 22 million UK customers at its 2025 full-year results, published on 5 March 2026, with group general insurance premiums up 18% to £14,145m and the UK and Ireland general insurance book up 27% to £9,787m at an undiscounted combined operating ratio of 94.1%. Its own repair network put more than 73,000 vehicles back on the road during 2025, and work done through that network is guaranteed for as long as you keep the car rather than for a fixed number of years.

The comprehensive wording is generous where it matters day to day. Personal belongings are covered to £500, tools to £500, non-manufacturer accessories to £1,000 a claim, and a child car seat is replaced after an impact even where nothing looks broken. Lost or stolen keys are met up to the market value of the car with no excess to pay, and being hit by an uninsured driver costs you neither your excess nor your claim-free years provided you can hand over the other registration. Aviva holds a 5 star Defaqto rating on its car product and says it was named a Which? recommended provider for car insurance in both 2025 and 2026.

sections.heading: What the published limits actually say
sections.html:
Aviva prints most of the numbers that matter in its product information document rather than burying them in a schedule you only see after buying, which makes the cover unusually easy to price against a rival before you commit. Motor injury protection pays £5,000 per person per period of insurance as standard; the optional Plus version lifts that to £120,000 and adds up to £500 each per claim towards physiotherapy. Recovery of a damaged car is met to £500, and motor legal services, if you add them, run to £100,000.

A car written off or stolen in its first 12 months is replaced with a new one where the damage comes to more than 60% of the UK list price, provided you were the first registered keeper and bought it new rather than as an ex-demonstrator. A courtesy car comes with comprehensive cover only and stays with you for the whole repair, or for up to 28 days if the car is stolen or declared a total loss. On the Aviva, Gold and Platinum tiers the loan car is a three-door hatchback, or a five-door on Platinum.

Trips into Europe are where the tiers diverge. The Signature wording allows any one trip of up to 90 days with a total across the year of six months, while the base Aviva tier allows 60 days a trip and Gold and Platinum allow 90 days. A car loaned to you while yours is off the road is covered for up to 7 days. Driving someone else's car on your own certificate is limited to policyholders aged 25 and over and gives third party cover only.

sections.heading: Electric and hybrid drivers get more than a footnote
sections.html:
Aviva treats the charging equipment as part of the car rather than as household kit, which is still not universal. Charging cables are covered in the vehicle, while in use, and while stored in a private garage. A wall box fitted in the garage is insured, and comprehensive policies extend to breakdown of a home charging point including the electrical wiring between the fuse box and the unit itself, up to £2,000 a claim.

Batteries held on a lease rather than owned outright are covered as standard. If the car is stolen or written off, Aviva settles the vehicle's value minus the battery and deals with the battery separately with the manufacturer, which avoids the settlement stalling while the two sides argue over who owns what. Run flat on charge and, on comprehensive cover, an RAC mechanic will either put in enough charge to reach a working point or move the car and up to seven passengers to a working charger or your home, whichever is nearer. Hybrids are excluded from that last one.

sections.heading: The regulator's own reading of why motor claims cost more
sections.html:
Any quote makes more sense against what the market is paying out, and the sharpest free source is the FCA's multi-firm review of motor claims costs, published in July 2025 and drawn from 12 insurers covering more than half the private motor market. Between 2019 and 2023 total claims costs rose 34%, an increase of £2.3bn. The average claim went from £2,410 to £3,293, and cost per policy from £309 to £391.

The detail explains the delays drivers notice. The average insured vehicle rose in value by 42%, from £9,319 to £13,223; the wait to get a car into a body shop more than doubled from 15 days to 31 days; and bodyshop labour rates climbed 28%, from £35 to £45 an hour. Theft claims grew 14% more frequent and 49% more expensive. Claims made against untraced and uninsured drivers cost the Motor Insurers' Bureau £452m in 2024 against £329m in 2019, roughly 2.78% of what an average driver pays.

The FCA's general insurance value measures, published on 21 July 2026 for calendar year 2025, show the other side of that. Motor premiums fell 7% across the market during 2025 while claims costs as a share of premium rose from 54% to 59%. A renewal quote that has not moved much is doing so against a market where insurers kept less of every pound.

sections.heading: The excesses that stack behind the headline price
sections.html:
Aviva's excess structure rewards using its own suppliers and charges you for going elsewhere, and the amounts are set out plainly enough that there is no excuse for being caught out. Glass repaired through the approved fitter costs a £10 excess and a replacement costs £115. Use a fitter of your own choosing and the payout is capped at £185 in total, which will not cover a modern windscreen carrying the cameras for lane assist and automatic braking, all of which need recalibrating once the glass is fitted.

The same principle applies to body repairs, where taking the car to your own garage rather than an approved one adds a specific £200 excess on top of whatever excess your schedule already carries. On third party, fire and theft the accessories limit drops from £1,000 to £100. Cancel inside the 14 day cooling-off period after cover has begun and there is a £38 charge plus insurance premium tax as well as the pro-rata deduction; cancel later and the same £38 applies.

Several headline figures are not published at all. Personal accident benefit, medical expenses and the compulsory excess itself all appear only as the amount "shown in your schedule", which means they depend on the tier and the quote and cannot be compared across insurers until you have gone through a full application. Aviva also sells motor cover under Signature, Aviva, Gold, Platinum and the separate Aviva Zero brand, so two quotes carrying the same logo are not necessarily the same contract.

sections.heading: What Aviva's own complaints figures show
sections.html:
Firms of this size have to publish their complaints data, and Aviva's is on its own website rather than buried elsewhere. For the half year from 1 July to 31 December 2025, Aviva Insurance Limited opened 49,795 general insurance complaints, a rate of 2.72 per 1,000 policies. It closed 43.5% within three working days and a further 54.2% between three days and eight weeks. The uphold rate was 52.6%, meaning slightly more than half of everyone who complained was found to have had a point. The most common subject was general administration and customer service rather than a declined claim.

A complaint that cannot be settled goes to the Financial Ombudsman Service free of charge, at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR, and Aviva is bound by its decisions while you are not. Ombudsman figures for the first half of 2025 record 1,463 new complaints about Aviva Insurance Limited across general insurance and protection, against an overall uphold rate of 32% in the consumer's favour, down from 35% a year earlier. Aviva's motor complaints line is 0345 030 6984, with claims complaints on 0345 030 6925. Should the insurer be unable to meet its obligations, the Financial Services Compensation Scheme may cover the shortfall.

pros: Personal belongings to £500, tools to £500 and accessories to £1,000 as standard on comprehensive
Repairs through Aviva's approved network are guaranteed for as long as you own the car
Charging cables, garage wall boxes and home charging point breakdown covered to £2,000 for EV drivers
Key replacement up to the car's market value with no excess
Uninsured driver promise refunds the excess and protects claim-free years
Most limits published in the product information document rather than hidden in a schedule
5 star Defaqto rating on the car product
cons: More than half of complaints go the customer's way: Aviva Insurance Limited upheld 52.6% of the 49,795 general insurance complaints it opened in the second half of 2025
Using your own body shop instead of an approved repairer adds a £200 excess, and glass fitted outside the network is capped at £185 against an industry average windscreen repair well above that
Personal accident benefit, medical expenses and the compulsory excess are only ever quoted as the amount shown in your schedule, so they cannot be compared before you apply
A £38 charge plus tax applies even inside the 14 day cooling-off period once cover has started
Driving other cars is restricted to policyholders aged 25 and over and gives third party cover only
European use on the base Aviva tier is limited to 60 days a trip against 90 on Gold and Platinum
Standard motor injury protection is only £5,000 per person unless you pay for the Plus version
verdict: Aviva sells a well-documented comprehensive policy from a balance sheet that few UK insurers can match, and it publishes more of its limits up front than most. The value sits in the repair network, the lifetime guarantee on its own workmanship and the electric vehicle cover, all of which are worth real money on a claim. The catch is that the price you see depends on which Aviva door you walked through, and that several of the numbers you would want for a like-for-like comparison only appear on your schedule. Get the quote, then read the schedule against the excesses set out above before you agree to it.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites an Aviva car insurance policy?
faqs.a: Aviva Insurance Limited, registered in Scotland under number SC002116 with its registered office at Pitheavlis, Perth PH2 0NH. It is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and the PRA under firm reference 202153, which you can check yourself on the Financial Services Register. Policies sold through Aviva's online arm are arranged by Aviva UK Digital Limited, firm reference 728985.

faqs.q: What does Aviva charge to replace a windscreen?
faqs.a: A repair carries a £10 excess and a full replacement a £115 excess when the work goes through Aviva's approved glass supplier. If you use a fitter of your own, the most Aviva will pay towards the job is £185 in total, so on any modern screen with driver assistance cameras behind it you would be covering the balance yourself.

faqs.q: Am I covered driving in Europe?
faqs.a: Yes, at least to the minimum required by law in the listed countries, but the length of stay depends on the tier. The Signature wording allows a single trip of up to 90 days with six months in total across the year. The base Aviva tier allows 60 days per trip, and Gold and Platinum allow 90 days. Trips beyond the minimum legal cover need the separate motoring in Europe extension.

faqs.q: Will Aviva give me a new car if mine is written off?
faqs.a: Only in the first 12 months from new, and only if the repair cost or damage exceeds 60% of the vehicle's UK list price, or if the car is stolen and not recovered. You must have been the first registered keeper. Ex-demonstrators and nearly new cars are excluded from the replacement clause.

faqs.q: How do I complain about Aviva, and does it get me anywhere?
faqs.a: Motor complaints go to 0345 030 6984, or claims complaints to 0345 030 6925, or in writing to Building 8, Maxim Business Park, Eurocentral ML1 4WR. If eight weeks pass or you are unhappy with the answer, the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR will look at it free of charge on 0800 023 4567. Aviva's published figures for the second half of 2025 show 52.6% of complaints upheld in the customer's favour, so it is worth pursuing.

title: Aviva Landlord Insurance Review
meta_title: Aviva Landlord Insurance: Unlimited Cover, Three Properties
meta_description: Aviva covers up to three rental homes with no cap on the buildings sum insured. What the wording promises, what the schedule decides, and where it stops.
intro:
Aviva is the largest general insurer in the country and its landlord policy is one of the few that will not put a ceiling on the building. Cover is sold under the AvivaPlus name direct from aviva.co.uk, and the headline is an unlimited buildings and contents sum insured — no rebuild figure to guess at, no under-insurance argument after a fire. Three conditions come with it: the property must have five bedrooms or fewer, be built of brick, stone, slate or tile, and not be listed. Most terraced and semi-detached lets clear all three without trying.

The policy is written by Aviva Insurance Limited, registered in Scotland number 2116, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the PRA and the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 202153 — a number printed on the product documents themselves and checkable on the FCA Register. Subsidence and flood are in the standard cover rather than sold on. So is loss of rent or the cost of rehousing a tenant when insured damage makes the house unlivable, cover for contents in garages and outbuildings inside the boundary, replacement locks after keys are lost or stolen, and matching-set replacement when a damaged item in a suite cannot be paired. Employers' liability is included for anyone you employ around the property, which catches the cleaner and the gardener that landlords routinely forget.

Scale is the other half of the case. Aviva's half-year results on 14 August 2026 showed general insurance premiums of £8,093 million, up 29% year on year, an operating profit of £1,326 million and a UK and Ireland combined operating ratio of 93.4% — a company taking in comfortably more than it pays out, which is what you want from the firm holding your building. It serves 21.8 million customers in the UK. A landlord claim here is not going to a business that might not be there in five years.

sections.heading: Aviva now owns both sides of your shortlist
sections.html:
Something changed in this market on 1 July 2025 that has not filtered through to most landlord advice: Aviva completed its purchase of Direct Line Group. Direct Line, Churchill, Privilege and the rest of that stable now sit inside the same parent as Aviva. By the August 2026 results Aviva had banked £100 million of run-rate cost savings against a £225 million ambition, with over £350 million of capital synergies targeted by the end of 2026.

For a landlord ringing round for quotes, that is worth knowing before you spend an afternoon on it. Getting a price from Aviva and a price from Direct Line no longer samples two independent balance sheets; it samples two brands and two pricing models under one owner. The quotes will still differ, sometimes by a lot, because the underwriting engines and distribution costs behind them have not merged. But the diversification a cautious landlord thinks they are buying by splitting a portfolio across those two names is thinner than it looks, and a genuine third opinion now has to come from outside that group.

sections.heading: Unlimited buildings cover, with three conditions attached
sections.html:
The unlimited sum insured is the strongest single feature of this policy and it solves a real problem. Rebuild costs have run well ahead of house prices; the Association of British Insurers recorded an average household claim of £6,340 in the first quarter of 2026, up 20% in a year, with weather damage averaging £6,040 and theft £4,350. A landlord who set a buildings figure five years ago and let it index along is quite likely under-insured now, and the usual consequence is a proportionate reduction in the payout rather than a refusal. Removing the figure removes the argument.

The conditions are where it bites. Five bedrooms or fewer rules out the larger house in multiple occupation. Brick, stone, slate or tile rules out timber-frame, thatch and a good deal of 1960s system-built stock. Unlisted rules out period property in conservation areas, which is a substantial slice of the private rented sector in older towns. If a let fails any of the three, this is not the policy for it and the quote engine will say so rather than pricing it up.

Cover excludes wet and dry rot, frost damage, gradual deterioration, manufacturing defects and storm damage to fences, gates and hedges. None of those is unusual, but the fence exclusion catches people out after every winter gale, and on a let property the tenant tends to report it as though it were covered.

sections.heading: The boiler cover carries the numbers the main policy doesn't
sections.html:
Aviva's Landlord Combined home emergency add-on is unusually well documented, and for a landlord it may be the more useful purchase of the two. It pays up to £4,000 per claim with no cap on the number of claims in a year, above a £50 excess. Gas central heating breakdown is unlimited per claim as long as the boiler is not beyond economical repair. It covers water supply pipes, plumbing and drainage, internal gas pipes, electrical wiring emergencies, and emergency security work such as boarding up, lock replacement and tarpaulin on a roof. The annual CP12 gas safety inspection and a boiler service are included, which is a legal obligation on every landlord in England and Wales turned into a covered cost.

Two numbers to hold on to. There is a 14-day exclusion period at the start, so a new policy bought the week a boiler starts making noises will not answer — first-year cover is roughly 11 and a half months. And if the boiler is seven years old or over and beyond economical repair, the payment is a flat £200 towards a replacement rather than the replacement itself. Under seven years, it replaces. The boiler must be natural gas and rated under 60 kW.

Guttering, soakaways, showers, household appliances, chimneys, pests and unvented cylinders are all outside it, as is a boiler that works but is noisy.

sections.heading: What changes when you buy the fourth flat
sections.html:
Aviva will put up to three rental properties on the direct policy. Its own page sends anyone with more than three to a broker, and the product waiting there is not a bigger version of the same thing — it is the commercial Property Owners wording, and the terms are meaningfully different.

On the version Aviva's brokers circulate, loss of rent is written as 30% of the buildings sum insured with a maximum indemnity period of 36 months, trace and access is capped at £50,000, replacement locks at £50,000, glass at £2,000 in aggregate, recycling costs within debris removal at £10,000 and gardening equipment at £10,000. Employers' liability appears at £5,000,000. A building counts as unoccupied after 90 consecutive days, and once it is long-term unoccupied the wording demands documented inspections at least every 7 days, external openings locked and sealed, services off at the mains or heating held above 4°C, and combustible material cleared. Dishonesty by an employee has to be discovered within seven working days of the act to be claimable.

The quieter change is regulatory. The FCA's pricing rules in PS21/5 — the ones that stopped renewal quotes being priced above what a new customer pays — apply to insurance sold to consumers. A commercial property owners' policy sits outside them, so the renewal discipline you get on the direct product is not automatic on the broker one. Ombudsman access mostly survives the move: the Financial Ombudsman Service takes complaints from businesses turning over less than £6.5 million with a balance sheet under £5 million or fewer than 50 staff, which covers almost every private landlord, and its award limit rose to £455,000 on 1 April 2026 for acts on or after 1 April 2019. Worth checking rather than assuming, because the protection changes shape at exactly the point most people stop reading.

One landlord-specific clause survives in both: liability under the Defective Premises Act follows you for up to seven years after you sell the property. Selling a let does not close the file.

sections.heading: A wording that tells you almost nothing until the schedule arrives
sections.html:
Read the AvivaPlus landlord policy booklet cover to cover and you will not find a single pound figure. Public liability is "up to the limit shown on your schedule". The legal services section is "up to the amount shown on your schedule". Excesses are "the excess(es) shown on your schedule". The unoccupancy limit — the number that decides more landlord claims than any other — is "more than the period shown on your schedule". The product information document does the same. Compared with insurers who publish a £2 million or £5 million liability limit and a 45- or 60-day void period on the face of the document, Aviva makes it impossible to compare this policy against another one until you have run a full quote and read the schedule that comes back.

That is defensible underwriting — the limits genuinely are set risk by risk — and it is poor disclosure. It also means the comparison tables that quote an Aviva landlord liability limit are inferring it. Get the schedule, read the four numbers above, and only then put it next to a rival quote. There is no published starting price for the landlord product either, which is the one place AXA and Admiral are more forthcoming.

Aviva's own Defaqto five-star rating is quoted against its home insurance on the landlord page rather than against the landlord product itself. A separate landlord star rating could not be confirmed from Aviva's own material and should be treated as unverified.

sections.heading: The gap between what tenants do and what the policy pays
sections.html:
Three exclusions sit uncomfortably close to the risks that actually define letting. Theft, attempted theft, malicious damage and vandalism by your tenants are excluded — not capped, excluded. Insurers that do cover it tend to cap it around £5,000; Aviva's direct wording does not reach it at all. A stripped property at the end of a bad tenancy is a cost you carry.

Accidental damage is an optional extra, covering things like a cracked bath, sink, toilet or window. Aviva's own claims analysis, published in April 2026 and covering January 2022 to March 2026, found accidental damage to be the single largest category at 32% of home claims, with the average payout up 63% from £1,148 in 2022 to £1,869. The most common cause was a television. Leaving off the cheapest add-on to the most frequent claim type is a false economy on a property somebody else lives in.

And there is no rent guarantee at any price. The loss of rent in the policy answers after insured damage, not after a tenant stops paying — a distinction that matters more since Section 21 possession ended on 1 May 2026 under the Renters' Rights Act 2025 and arrears cases began taking longer. Arrears cover has to be bought elsewhere.

On complaints, Aviva Insurance Limited published 2.72 complaints per 1,000 policies for the six months to 31 December 2025, closing 43.5% within three days and upholding 52.6%. The leading cause was general administration and customer service rather than claims decisions. A high uphold rate cuts both ways: it says a lot of complaints were justified, and it says complaining to Aviva is better than even odds of getting somewhere without going further. If it does go further, the Ombudsman is free.

One thing nobody can tell you: the regulator's general insurance value measures release of 21 July 2026 reports claims acceptance by product line, and landlord and property owners' cover is not one of the lines. Buildings insurance for owner-occupiers came in at a 62% acceptance rate against motor's 99%, but that is a different product. Any acceptance rate quoted for landlord cover, for Aviva or anyone else, has been inferred rather than published.

pros: Unlimited buildings and contents sum insured on standard-construction homes of five bedrooms or fewer, which removes the under-insurance risk entirely
Subsidence, flood, loss of rent and tenant rehousing are all in the standard cover rather than sold as extras
Employers' liability included for cleaners, gardeners and anyone else you employ at the property
Home emergency add-on pays £4,000 a claim with unlimited claims, a £50 excess, and includes the annual CP12 gas safety check
Backed by the UK's largest general insurer: £8,093m of GI premiums in the first half of 2026 and a 93.4% UK combined operating ratio
No charge for updating personal details or making changes to the policy
cons: Theft, attempted theft, malicious damage and vandalism by your own tenants are excluded outright, not merely capped

The policy wording publishes no limits at all — liability, excesses, legal cover and the unoccupancy period are all "as shown on your schedule", so the policy cannot be compared with a rival until you have a full quote
Accidental damage is an optional extra even though it is 32% of Aviva's home claims at an average of £1,869
No rent guarantee is sold at any price, and loss of rent only responds after insured damage
Only three rental properties per policy; a fourth pushes you to a broker and the commercial Property Owners wording, where the FCA's consumer pricing rules no longer apply
Aviva Insurance Limited upheld 52.6% of complaints in the six months to 31 December 2025, and no starting price is published for the landlord product
Five-bedroom limit, standard construction and unlisted status rule out HMOs, timber-frame and period property in conservation areas
verdict: The right policy for a landlord with one to three ordinary brick-built houses who wants the rebuild risk taken off the table completely — the unlimited sum insured is genuinely valuable and few rivals match it. Add the accidental damage extra and the £4,000 home emergency cover, because between them they answer most of what actually goes wrong in a let. Read the schedule properly before you compare the price with anything, since the booklet will not tell you the limits. Buy rent guarantee somewhere else, and expect a different contract entirely the day you buy a fourth property.

faqs.q: How many rental properties can I put on one Aviva landlord policy?
faqs.a: Three. Aviva's own landlord page says you can cover up to three rental properties, and directs anyone with more to buy commercial cover through a broker. That broker product is the Property Owners wording, which carries different limits — loss of rent at 30% of the buildings sum insured over a 36-month indemnity period, a 90-day unoccupancy threshold and 7-day inspection requirements once a property is long-term empty.

faqs.q: Does Aviva really offer an unlimited buildings sum insured?
faqs.a: Yes, subject to three eligibility conditions: the property must have five bedrooms or fewer, be of standard construction in brick or stone with a slate or tile roof, and not be listed. Meet all three and there is no rebuild figure to estimate and no proportionate reduction for under-insurance. Fail any one and the property is not eligible for this policy.

faqs.q: Am I covered if my tenant damages or strips the property?
faqs.a: No. Theft, attempted theft, malicious damage and vandalism by your tenants are excluded from the AvivaPlus landlord policy. This is the exclusion most likely to cost a landlord real money, and it is worth pricing against insurers who cover it — usually with a cap in the region of £5,000 — before deciding on price alone. A deposit and a thorough inventory are doing that job here.

faqs.q: What does the Aviva home emergency add-on actually pay?
faqs.a: Up to £4,000 per claim with no limit on the number of claims in a year, above a £50 excess, covering plumbing and drainage, water and internal gas supply pipes, electrical emergencies, emergency security work and gas central heating breakdown, plus the annual CP12 inspection and boiler service. There is a 14-day wait before cover starts. If the boiler is seven years or older and beyond economical repair, you get £200 towards a new one rather than a replacement.

faqs.q: How long can the property stand empty between tenants?
faqs.a: On the direct policy the wording will not say — the limit is whatever appears on your schedule, and certain losses such as burst pipes and malicious damage fall away past it. On the broker Property Owners wording a building is unoccupied after 90 consecutive days, and long-term unoccupied property must be inspected at least every 7 days with a log kept, secured, cleared of combustibles and either drained at the mains or kept above 4°C. Find your own number and diary it the day the keys come back.

faqs.q: Who regulates Aviva and how do I complain?
faqs.a: Aviva Insurance Limited is registered in Scotland number 2116, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and PRA, firm reference 202153, verifiable on the FCA Register. Complain to Aviva first — 0800 158 4091 for claims, 0800 656 9717 otherwise. If you are unhappy with the answer, or eight weeks pass without one, the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR will review it free of charge. Its maximum award rose to £455,000 on 1 April 2026 for acts or omissions on or after 1 April 2019.

title: Aviva Over 50s Life Insurance Review
meta_title: Aviva Over 50s Life Insurance: What £5 to £100 a Month Buys
meta_description: Aviva's over 50s cover is guaranteed acceptance for ages 50 to 80, from £5 a month, with premiums stopping at 30 years or age 90. Figures, limits and gaps.
intro:
Aviva has been selling guaranteed acceptance life cover to older customers for decades, and the current version is about as straightforward as this kind of policy gets. Anyone aged between 50 and 80 who lives in the UK can take it out. There is no medical, no health questionnaire and no way to be turned down. You pick either the monthly premium you want to pay or the lump sum you want paid out, anywhere between £5 and £100 a month, and the figure you agree on the day you buy is the figure that comes out of your bank account for as long as you pay it. Aviva rates the cover 5 Stars with Defaqto on its own product page.

The structure is worth understanding before you get a quote, because it is unusual. Premiums are not for life. They stop after 30 years, or on the policy anniversary after your 90th birthday, whichever arrives first — and the cover carries on until you die regardless. Buy at 50 and you pay for thirty years; buy at 80 and you pay for ten. The cover amount itself is fixed on day one and never moves. Aviva throws in access to DigiCare+, its health app, which covers digital GP appointments, mental health support, nutrition advice and bereavement support at no extra charge, and there is currently an Amazon.co.uk gift card of up to £200 once you have paid six monthly premiums.

Behind it sits Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, company number 3253947, firm reference number 185896 on the Financial Conduct Authority register. The parent, Aviva plc, reported over 25 million customers and operating profit of £2,203 million for 2025 in results published on 5 March 2026, up 25% on the £1,767 million it made in 2024.
