sections.heading: What the £5.20 headline is measuring
sections.html:
The asterisk matters. Hiscox defines that price as an average of all public liability policies sold to at least 10% of its customer base between April 2025 and April 2026. It is the typical price paid by the largest slice of its book, not a floor and not an entry rate. A landscaper hauling equipment between third-party gardens is a different risk from a bookkeeper, and Hiscox lists the things that move the number: turnover, trade hazard, premises, whether you work at customers' sites, your safety record, the limit you pick and the extras you bolt on.

The liability wording itself is more generous than the price suggests in places. Defence costs are covered alongside the claim. If you are called to court over a covered matter, Hiscox pays compensation for the time — £250 a day for you, a partner or a director, £100 a day for any other employee, capped at £10,000 across the policy year. Products claims carry their own single aggregate limit and their own excess rather than sharing the main one, and pollution claims sit under a further aggregate that also swallows their defence costs.

Two figures are absent from every public page: the excess and the standard limit tiers. The wording repeatedly says both are "shown in the schedule", so you will not know what you are carrying until the quote is in front of you. Most trade contracts and local authority frameworks specify a limit in writing, so check that number before you buy rather than after.

sections.heading: Assembling the cover one module at a time
sections.html:
The parts on offer are professional indemnity to £10 million, public and products liability, employers' liability, tool and portable equipment cover, cyber and data, legal protection for contract disputes and debt recovery, personal accident, equipment breakdown and business contents. Personal accident is the one to read twice: the cover responds once you have been unable to work for more than two weeks, so a fortnight off with a broken wrist produces nothing.

There is one honest gap and Hiscox flags it plainly. On the trades page, under tool insurance for builders, the site says: "Hiscox doesn't provide this cover. But we can connect you to our builders' insurance partner today." A builder can still buy liability here; the kit in the van goes somewhere else, on someone else's terms, with a second renewal date to remember.

Contract works — the cover that pays for the half-built extension if it burns down before handover — is not described on any of the construction and trades pages. Given that JCT and similar contracts routinely require it, a builder or main contractor should confirm directly with Hiscox whether it can be added rather than assume the absence is an oversight. We could not verify it from the published material.

sections.heading: Who is actually carrying the risk
sections.html:
The policy is written by Hiscox Insurance Company Limited, registered number 70234, at 22 Bishopsgate, London EC2N 4BQ. It is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the FCA and the PRA, under firm reference number 113849 — a number you can put into the FCA Register yourself. The sales and administration side runs through Hiscox Underwriting Ltd, registered number 02372789 at the same address and regulated by the FCA. Because the insurer and the seller are parts of the same group, there is no broker commission layered on top and no panel deciding which insurer sees your details.

Complaints go first to Hiscox Customer Relations at The Hiscox Building, Peasholme Green, York YO1 7PR, on 0800 116 4627. A firm under the Ombudsman's size ceiling — £6.5 million turnover, fewer than 50 staff, or a balance sheet below £5 million — can take an unresolved complaint on to the Financial Ombudsman Service, provided the act complained of happened on or after 1 April 2019. Cancellation runs on 30 days' written notice with a pro rata refund of the unused premium, and Hiscox states it never charges a fee for cancelling. The general terms also mention a £20 minimum in this context, which is worth pinning down before you cancel part way through a year.

sections.heading: The clauses that decide whether a claim is paid
sections.html:
Notification is tight. A bodily injury claim must reach Hiscox within seven days. Anything else must be reported promptly and confirmed in writing within 30 days. You must not admit liability without prior written agreement, which sounds obvious until a customer is standing in a flooded kitchen waiting for you to say it was your fault.

The wording is also explicit that putting the work right is your bill, not the insurer's: you must take reasonable steps to remedy or rectify, at your own expense, any defect or failure. Liability cover pays for the damage your mistake causes to other people and their property. It does not pay to redo the job. Alongside that sit exclusions for designs, plans, specifications or advice you have given, for the cost of recalling, repairing or replacing a product you supplied, for asbestos, for anything you do deliberately or recklessly, and for pollution unless it came from a sudden, identifiable and unintended incident. Work carried out beyond the geographical limits on your schedule is outside the policy altogether.

Tool cover has its own trap. If the sum you insure is less than 85% of what your equipment is actually worth, any payout is reduced in proportion — insure £4,000 of a £6,000 kit and you are carrying a third of every claim yourself. Theft from an unattended vehicle is excluded unless the items were hidden out of sight in a locked boot or compartment, and unexplained disappearance is not covered at all. Settlement is on a replace-as-new basis for equipment and trade market value for stock, and cover can run UK-only, EU-wide or worldwide depending on what you select.

sections.heading: Reading the badges on the awards page
sections.html:
Hiscox displays a Defaqto five-star rating and it is genuine, but it belongs to the home insurance product, held for 14 consecutive years — not to the liability cover a tradesperson buys. Its own business pages muddle this further, one citing five stars for eleven years and another for fourteen. The Feefo Platinum Trusted Service award for 2026, a seventh consecutive year, sits alongside a 4.8 out of 5 score from 3,888 reviews. The customer-count figures do not line up either: the public liability page claims 460,000 UK businesses, while the main business insurance page says 300,000 small business customers. Both are Hiscox's own pages.

Independent claims data is thinner than it looks. The FCA published its general insurance value measures for calendar year 2025 on 21 July 2026, covering claims acceptance rates and complaints for retail lines — home sits at 62–71% acceptance and motor at 99%. Commercial and liability products are not in that dataset at all, so no published acceptance rate exists for the cover under discussion, from Hiscox or anyone else. Anybody quoting one for tradesman insurance has borrowed it from a different product.

What does exist is Hiscox's own regulatory complaints return. For 1 January to 30 June 2026 it opened 529 complaints and closed 541, with 11% resolved inside three days and the remaining 89% inside eight weeks. Of those closed, 57% were upheld in the customer's favour, and the leading cause was claims handling. The volume is low against the book — 0.86 complaints per 1,000 policies in force — but a majority upheld rate is a majority upheld rate, and it is the company's own published figure. Longer memories will also recall the Supreme Court ruling of January 2021 on pandemic business interruption, where Hiscox was among the insurers whose small-business policies were construed against them.

pros: Direct from the insurer with no broker fee or panel in between, and an online quote in around five minutes
Public liability from £5.20 a month with limits available up to £10 million
Defence costs covered alongside the claim, plus court attendance compensation of £250 a day for a director or partner up to a £10,000 annual cap
Underwritten by Hiscox Insurance Company Limited, FCA and PRA regulated under firm reference 113849, with a Lloyd's pedigree dating to 1901
Cancellation on 30 days' notice with a pro rata refund and no cancellation fee
Tools cover settles equipment as new, with UK, EU or worldwide territorial options
cons: Hiscox upheld 57% of the 541 complaints it closed in the first half of 2026, with claims handling the main cause — its own published figure
Builders are sent to a third-party partner for tool cover, so the kit in the van is insured by someone else on separate terms
The £5.20 a month headline is an average across the segment Hiscox sells most to between April 2025 and April 2026, not a starting price anyone is guaranteed
Tool cover carries an 85% average clause: undervalue your equipment and every payout is cut in proportion
No excess figures or standard limit tiers are published anywhere — both appear only on the schedule after you have quoted
The Defaqto five-star badge on the awards page is for home insurance, not for the business or liability products, and two Hiscox pages disagree on how many years it has held it
Contract works cover is not described on any of the trades pages, which matters for anyone signing a JCT contract
verdict: Hiscox suits the lighter trades — the electrician, the decorator, the kitchen fitter — who want to buy liability cover directly from the company carrying the risk, at a known price, without a broker in the chain. The wording is clear, the regulatory position is unambiguous, and the £10 million limit covers most contractual demands. The trade-off is that you are the one assembling the policy: nobody checks that your tools sum is within 85% of their value, that your limit matches the framework you are bidding into, or that a builder's equipment has ended up with a different insurer. Read the schedule when it arrives, and price the modules you actually need rather than the one in the advert.

faqs.q: How much is Hiscox public liability for a tradesperson?
faqs.a: Cover starts at £5.20 a month, but that figure is an average of policies sold to at least 10% of the Hiscox customer base between April 2025 and April 2026 rather than a guaranteed entry price. Tool cover is priced separately from £7.20 a month. Your own quote moves on turnover, trade, whether you work at customers' premises, your safety record and the limit you choose.

faqs.q: What liability limit do I need?
faqs.a: Hiscox offers up to £10 million. The right number is usually set for you rather than by you: main contractors, letting agents and local authority frameworks name a required limit in the contract, and £5 million is common for construction work. Check the contract wording before buying, because a cheaper policy at a lower limit is no use if the job will not accept it.

faqs.q: Does Hiscox cover my tools?
faqs.a: For most trades, yes, through portable equipment cover settling on a replace-as-new basis, with UK, EU or worldwide options. Builders are the exception — Hiscox says it does not provide that cover and refers them to a partner. Insure the full value: fall below 85% of what the kit is worth and claims are reduced proportionally. Theft from an unattended vehicle only counts if the items were locked out of sight.

faqs.q: Who regulates Hiscox and what happens if a claim is refused?
faqs.a: Policies are underwritten by Hiscox Insurance Company Limited, firm reference 113849, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and PRA. Complaints go first to Hiscox Customer Relations in York on 0800 116 4627. If that does not resolve it, a business with turnover under £6.5 million and fewer than 50 employees can refer the matter to the Financial Ombudsman Service, for acts on or after 1 April 2019.

title: Hostelling International Hostels: Membership, Booking Terms and What HI Actually Runs
meta_title: Hostelling International Hostels: Membership and Prices
meta_description: What HI membership costs in Britain, the 10% member discount, the 24-hour cancellation rule, and how far the HI quality audit really reaches.
intro:
Hostelling International is the federation that a great many British travellers have used without ever learning its name. Its member associations run more than 2,300 hostels, it counts “more than 2,63 million members from around the world”, and it traces the network back to a German schoolteacher, Richard Schirrmann, who opened the first youth hostel in his own school at Altena in Westphalia in 1914. The federation itself was founded in 1932 as the International Youth Hostel Federation, adopted the Hostelling International name in 2006, and still describes itself as working “for Good, Not For Profit”. In England and Wales its member association is YHA; in Scotland it is Hostelling Scotland. Both are registered charities, and a card bought from either one works across the whole federation.

What separates HI from an ordinary bed-booking site is that it publishes a standard and pays somebody outside the organisation to check it. Hostels in the HI Quality & Sustainability programme are, in HI's own words, “certified every 3 years by an external auditor”, and the management system behind that programme is recognised by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council. The GSTC's published register lists it as “HI-Q&S (Hostelling International Quality and Sustainability Management System)”, owner Hostelling International, United Kingdom, version 1 July 2018, with recognition dates of 14 January 2016 and 16 June 2019. Very few accommodation brands of any size submit to a fixed outside audit cycle at all.

One structural point is better known before you book than after. HI runs the search and takes the deposit, but it is not the party selling you the bed. Its own booking terms say so without hedging: “Booking made on hihostels.com are a contract with the hostel or Youth Hostel Association who runs the hostel, not HI.” Nor do you have to join to use it — “You do not need to be a member…in order to make your booking” — although membership is compulsory at the door in some countries, and elsewhere non-members “pay a small surcharge or can purchase a membership card at the hostel”.

sections.heading: A federation of charities, not a hotel chain
sections.html:
The organisation behind hihostels.com is a British one, which surprises most people who assume a global hostel network must sit somewhere warmer. The International Youth Hostel Federation is company 02250706, incorporated on 3 May 1988 as a private company limited by guarantee without share capital, using the exemption that lets it drop “Limited” from its name. Its registered office is 7 Bell Yard, London WC2A 2JR, its SIC code is 94990 — activities of other membership organisations — and its last accounts were made up to 31 December 2025. Its own website terms of use put the position in one line: “the International Youth Hostel Federation (IYHF) operating as Hostelling International (“HI”)”, Registered Charity No. 1117014. The company has carried three names in its life, trading as HOSTELLING INTERNATIONAL between 3 April 2006 and 15 April 2010 and as IYHF TRUST before that.

Underneath the federation sit the national associations, and the British ones are older than the federation's UK company by half a century. YHA (England and Wales) is company 00282555, incorporated on 12 December 1933 as the Youth Hostels Trust of England and Wales Limited, registered at Trevelyon House, Dimple Road, Matlock, and filed under SIC 55202, which is the code for youth hostels and almost nothing else uses. Its stated charitable object has not been modernised into blandness: “To help all, especially young people of limited means, to a greater knowledge, love and care of the countryside, and appreciation of the cultural values of towns and cities.” Hostelling Scotland is the Scottish Youth Hostels Association, a Scottish charity registered with OSCR.

This matters for a practical reason rather than a sentimental one. A charity that owns its buildings prices differently from a platform that owns none, it publishes accounts you can read, and it has a reason to keep a hostel open in a valley that no commercial operator would touch. It also means the money you spend has a visible destination, which is unusual in online travel.

sections.heading: Who you are actually contracting with
sections.html:
HI's booking terms are short and, on the points that matter, unambiguous. The contract for the stay is with the hostel or the national association, not with HI. HI “collect[s] a non-refundable deposit payment at the time of booking” and the balance is settled with the hostel. Cancellation is free provided “the cancellation must be made at least 24 hours prior to the arrival time”, and the terms fix that arrival time for you whether or not you told anyone when you were turning up: “The arrival time at your destination hostel is considered as 18:00 (6pm) local time to the hostel.” In practice that means a booking for a Saturday has to be cancelled by 18:00 on the Friday.

Miss that and the charge is set out plainly. “If a cancellation is not received and you do not arrive for a booking of 1 night you will be charged 1 night, plus applicable taxes. If a cancellation is not received and you do not arrive for a booking of 2 or more nights you will be charged 2 nights, plus applicable taxes.” Even where you cancel in time, “the booking deposit is always non-refundable, unless stated otherwise in the booking conditions”.

The limitation of liability follows from the same structure and is worth reading twice: “In the event of a problem arising, our liability, if any, is limited to the fees paid by you on this website.” Since what you pay on the website is the deposit, that is the ceiling on any claim against HI itself. Disputes about the room, the cleanliness or the money you paid on arrival belong with the hostel and its association. The terms are governed by “the laws of England and Wales” and “[t]he courts of England and Wales shall have exclusive jurisdiction”, which is a genuine convenience for a British reader booking a bed in Ljubljana and a point most international booking platforms do not offer.

sections.heading: What a card costs in Britain, and what it takes off the bill
sections.html:
HI's own site is coy about price. The membership pages say only that “[p]rices vary depending on your place of residence” and that a membership “is valid for 12 months” from the date of purchase; the actual figure appears nowhere on hihostels.com. For a British buyer the number comes from the national association, and it is small.

YHA charges £20 a year for adult membership paid by direct debit and £10 a year for ages 16 to 25, and the return is “10% off every booking including pre-booked breakfast”. Under-26s get “an additional 5% discount…stacked on top of your 10% discount”. Hostelling Scotland runs a longer ladder, with rates that “apply from 5 April” and are “non-refundable”: £15 per annum for adults aged 26 and over, £6 per annum for a young person aged 25 or under, £150 for life, £30 per annum for groups of ten or more, £25 per booking for a temporary group, and £3 per overnight if you would rather not join at all.

On a £25 dorm bed, 10% is £2.50, so a £20 YHA card pays for itself over eight nights, or over roughly five for a 21-year-old stacking the extra 5%. A Scottish £6 young person's card pays for itself faster still. Two conditions attach. “Individual adults (over 16) must have their own membership” unless a family or group card covers them, and membership becomes “non-refundable, non-transferable to another person after activation”, with cancellation permitted but carrying no refund. Buying the card through a third party is the one route HI warns against: “If you book through an online travel agent or 3rd party, we cannot guarantee your HI membership will be honoured.”

sections.heading: The standard behind the badge, and how far it reaches
sections.html:
HI-Q&S is the best thing on the site and it is undersold. It is described as “a long-term programme of continuous improvement that allows hostels and associations to advance their quality and sustainability practices”, hostels are “certified every 3 years by an external auditor”, and the management system is GSTC-recognised. The federation's About page goes further and tells the reader that “all our hostels meet the HI standards, which guarantee a range of good quality safe accommodation, in friendly surroundings at affordable prices”.

The programme's own page gives the scale, and it does not match that sentence. “HI-Q&S is used in 32 Associations and over 400 Hostels worldwide.” Against a network of more than 2,300 hostels and 57 or 58 associations, that is a little over one hostel in six and roughly half the associations. The audit is real, the coverage is partial, and only the first of those two facts is advertised.

There is a British yardstick to set beside it, and no hostel listing on hihostels.com carries it. VisitEngland runs a dedicated hostel assessment scheme in which “[o]ne of our professional assessors will visit as a mystery guest”, and it publishes the standards in full. Minimum entry requires self-catering facilities, wet clothing storage, daily cleaning, a first aid kit and emergency contact information; bedrooms need “a minimum floor space per bed (or bunk) of 4 square metres”, a two-metre ceiling, an external window and beds “at least 1.9m (6'3") x 0.76m (2'6")”; kitchens need “a minimum of 4 cooking rings”. Star bands run 60–74% for three stars, 75–86% for four and 87–100% for five, with sectional floors underneath — four stars requires “no area to score less than 67%” and a “cleanliness minimum score 76%”. The scheme also runs two lower tiers, Quality Assessed and Visitor Ready, and states that “[n]ot all types of hostel are given a star rating, but all of them must meet a set of minimum requirements”. If a hostel you are considering in England holds one of those ratings, it is worth more than any score collected by the seller, and HI does not show it.

sections.heading: Booking a bed is not a package holiday
sections.html:
Two pieces of British law shape what you get when you press the button, and neither is mentioned on the site. The first is the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018, which define a package as “a combination of at least two different types of travel services for the purpose of the same trip or holiday”, the types being “the carriage of passengers; the provision of accommodation; the rental of cars, other motor vehicles, or motorcycles; [or] any other tourist service”. A hostel bed on its own is one type, so a bed booked alone is not a package and carries none of the insolvency protection or organiser liability that a package carries. Nor is it an ATOL matter, because no flight is involved. Booking accommodation by itself is one of the least protected purchases in travel, and that is true of every hostel platform rather than of HI in particular.

That regime is about to move. The Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements (Amendment) Regulations 2026 come into force on 6 April 2027, remove the concept of linked travel arrangements altogether — the instrument directs simply “Omit regulation 26 (insolvency protection and information requirements for linked travel arrangements)” — widen the definition of a package to catch separate selections and separate payments made on “a single visit to, or contact with, the trader's point of sale”, and add a third-party refund obligation running to 14 days. A traveller who books a bed and a ferry in one sitting from one seller after that date may find themselves better protected than they are now.

The second piece of law explains the non-refundable deposit, and it is the answer to a complaint people often make unfairly. Regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 excludes from the ordinary cancellation right “the supply of accommodation, transport of goods, vehicle rental services, catering or services related to leisure activities, if the contract provides for a specific date or period of performance”. The 14-day right to change your mind that applies to almost everything else bought online — “the cancellation period ends at the end of 14 days after the day on which the contract is entered into” for a service — simply does not attach to a room booked for a named night. HI's 24-hour rule is therefore a concession rather than a legal minimum, and a more generous one than a good deal of the hotel market offers.

sections.heading: The case for going straight to the hostel
sections.html:
Filter hihostels.com to England and you will find roughly seventy properties spread over seven pages, and all but a handful of them are YHA. That is not a criticism of the search — YHA is the English member association, so of course they are its hostels — but it does change the arithmetic for a domestic trip, because YHA sells the same beds itself and says openly what the intermediary layer costs it.

YHA's own book-direct page states that “[l]ast year, about £2 million of YHA's income was absorbed by third party booking agents”, money the charity would rather “invest…in improving young people's health, wellbeing and life skills”. It offers a price undertaking that no aggregator matches: “If you find a better rate elsewhere online, we will refund the difference”, applying where within 24 hours of booking on yha.org.uk you find an equivalent offer for the same property at a lower price. It says the direct site carries “our complete range of accommodation” and is “[t]he only way to redeem promotional codes and take advantage of special offers”. And critically, the 10% member discount and the extra 5% for under-26s are described throughout as applying to bookings “made online at yha.org.uk”.

The sensible conclusion is not that the HI site is worthless but that it earns its keep in different places. Abroad, where you have no account with the Slovenian or Portuguese association and no idea which properties are affiliated, one search across the whole federation with one membership number behind it is genuinely useful, and the same card that costs £20 in Matlock works at the door in Lisbon. At home, where the operator is a charity you can book with directly, is running a best-rate refund, and is quietly losing about £2 million a year to intermediaries, the case for the middle layer is much weaker.

sections.heading: Numbers on the site that do not agree with each other
sections.html:
Read HI's pages side by side and the network changes size. The About HI page describes “58 Member Associations operating over 2,300 hostels in hundreds of amazing destinations”. The network directory on the same site describes “57 Member Associations with over 2,300 hostels as well as affiliate hostels in 2 destinations”. One association is a trivial difference; publishing both figures on one website is the sort of thing that makes a careful reader check everything else.

The bigger gap is between the federation and its own members. HI says over 2,300 hostels. YHA tells its members that their card gives “[a]ccess over 4,000 hostels through automatic Hostelling International membership” and, on its dedicated page, “over 4.000 hostels in 90 countries”. Hostelling Scotland says membership “gives you access to over 4,000 hostels around the world with dual membership of Hostelling International”. Two national associations advertise a network almost twice the size the federation claims for itself, and nothing on any of the three sites reconciles the two counts. The likeliest explanation is that the larger number sweeps in affiliated and partner properties that HI does not count as its own, but no page says so, and a reader choosing on network size is being given two different answers by the same organisation.

A third gap is smaller and easier to fix. The membership pages promise “thousands of travel discounts at home and abroad”. The benefits page lists six partners: 15% off an Airalo eSIM, 15% off luggage storage with Bounce, 10% off European shipments with Eurosender, up to 10% on selected products through DiscoverCars, 25% off pickpocket-proof travel garments from Clever Travel Companion, and free or tip-based tours through Freetour.com. It adds that “[m]ore benefits and discounts might be available at your destination”, which is doubtless true and is not the same as thousands.

One page has simply been left behind. A Covid-19 measures page marked “Updated June 2022” is still published, still tells readers that “[m]any hostels in our network now require guests to present a proof of COVID-19 vaccination and/or a negative test result”, and still describes a refund concession “designed to ensure we survive during this turbulent time”. Four years on, that page is a liability rather than a service.

For scale, the market these beds sit in is growing slowly rather than quickly. VisitBritain's inbound forecast published on 27 August 2026 expects 44.2 million inbound visits to the UK in 2026 spending £33.9 billion, growth of 2% in both visits and nominal spending but a 1% decline in spending in real terms, putting volume at 103% and nominal value at 119% of 2019 while real spend is still only 90% of the 2019 level. European markets are forecast to grow 4% by volume and 7% by value while long-haul markets fall 3% and 2%. Short-haul European visitors are exactly the market a hostel bed is priced for, and they are the part of the market that is still expanding.

pros: One membership and one search across a federation of more than 2,300 hostels and 57 to 58 national associations
Participating hostels are “certified every 3 years by an external auditor” under HI-Q&S, whose management system is recognised by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council
The federation is a UK registered charity (1117014) and its British members, YHA and Hostelling Scotland, are charities too
You do not need to join to book, and membership runs 12 months from the date of purchase rather than to a calendar year end
British membership is cheap: £20 a year at YHA, £10 for 16 to 25s, £15 at Hostelling Scotland and £6 for those aged 25 and under
A 10% member discount on YHA bookings, with a further 5% stacked on top for under-26s
Free cancellation up to 24 hours before an assumed 18:00 arrival, which is more generous than the law requires for a dated booking
Terms governed by the laws of England and Wales, with exclusive jurisdiction in the English courts
cons: The booking deposit is non-refundable in almost all circumstances and the terms never state what percentage of the price it is, so you cannot tell what you are risking until you reach the payment screen
HI's liability is “limited to the fees paid by you on this website” — that is, the deposit — because the stay itself is contracted with the hostel or national association rather than with HI
HI-Q&S covers “32 Associations and over 400 Hostels” out of a network of more than 2,300, while the About page tells readers that “all our hostels meet the HI standards”
The price of membership appears nowhere on hihostels.com; you have to go to a separate site or ask at the hostel door to find out what a card costs
HI's own pages give 57 and 58 member associations, and its British members advertise “over 4,000 hostels” against the federation's “over 2,300”, with nothing anywhere reconciling the two
“Thousands of travel discounts at home and abroad” turns out to be six named partners on the benefits page
A Covid-19 measures page last updated in June 2022 is still live and still tells travellers that many hostels require proof of vaccination or a negative test
Hostel listing pages show no nightly price until you enter dates and no independent quality rating at all, even where an English hostel holds a VisitEngland star rating
For a stay in England or Wales you are almost always booking a YHA hostel, and YHA's 10% member discount, promotional codes and best-rate refund apply only to bookings made at yha.org.uk
verdict: Hostelling International is a well-run federation doing something unusual: publishing a quality standard, paying an outside auditor to check it every three years, and putting the whole thing behind a UK charity with accounts anybody can read. For a trip through several countries, one £20 card and one search across 2,300-odd hostels is a genuinely good deal, and the 24-hour cancellation rule is more generous than the law obliges anyone to be on a dated booking. The site's weaknesses are of presentation rather than substance — a membership price it never quotes, a quality programme that reaches a sixth of the network while the marketing implies all of it, three different network sizes across the federation and its own members, and a pandemic page four years past its usefulness. And for a hostel in England or Wales, the operator is YHA, which will refund the difference if you find the bed cheaper elsewhere and loses about £2 million a year to intermediaries. Use HI abroad, where the federation is the point; think twice before using it to book a bed forty miles from home.

faqs.q: Do I have to be a member to book an HI hostel?
faqs.a: No. HI states that “[y]ou do not need to be a member…in order to make your booking”. In some countries membership is compulsory to stay, and in others non-members “pay a small surcharge or can purchase a membership card at the hostel”. Where it is optional, a card bought in advance earns the member rate on the booking itself.

faqs.q: What does HI membership cost in the UK?
faqs.a: HI does not publish a price on its own site — it says only that prices “vary depending on your place of residence”. You buy through the national association. YHA charges £20 a year by direct debit for adults and £10 a year for ages 16 to 25. Hostelling Scotland charges £15 a year for those aged 26 and over, £6 for those 25 and under, £150 for life membership and £3 per overnight for non-members, with rates applying from 5 April.

faqs.q: When can I cancel without being charged?
faqs.a: The cancellation must be made “at least 24 hours prior to the arrival time”, and HI's terms treat your arrival time as “18:00 (6pm) local time to the hostel” regardless of when you actually intended to turn up. The deposit is non-refundable either way. Fail to cancel and not turn up and you are charged one night on a one-night booking or two nights on any longer booking, plus taxes.

faqs.q: Is my money protected if the hostel goes under?
faqs.a: Not by the package travel rules. A package requires “a combination of at least two different types of travel services for the purpose of the same trip or holiday”, and a bed booked on its own is one service, so the insolvency protection and organiser liability in the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 do not apply. HI's own liability is capped at the fees you paid on its website. Paying by credit card, or holding travel insurance, is the practical answer.

faqs.q: Are HI hostels independently inspected?
faqs.a: Some are. Hostels in the HI Quality & Sustainability programme are “certified every 3 years by an external auditor” and the management system is recognised by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council, but the programme is “used in 32 Associations and over 400 Hostels worldwide” rather than across the whole network. In England there is a separate route: VisitEngland runs a hostel assessment scheme in which an assessor visits as a mystery guest, with star bands of 60–74%, 75–86% and 87–100%. HI does not display those ratings.

faqs.q: Should I book on hihostels.com or with the hostel directly?
faqs.a: Abroad, the HI search is genuinely useful and the membership discount travels with you. In England and Wales, the hostel is almost always YHA, which offers to “refund the difference” if you find a better rate online within 24 hours, applies its 10% member discount and 5% under-26 discount to bookings at yha.org.uk, and says direct booking is “the only way to redeem promotional codes and take advantage of special offers”. For a domestic stay, going direct is usually both cheaper and better for the charity.

title: Hostelworld Review: The Deposit, the Balance and What You Pay at the Door
meta_title: Hostelworld Review: What the Deposit Really Pays For
meta_description: Hostelworld lists around 17,000 hostels in 180+ countries. What the deposit covers, what you settle at the hostel, and how the guarantees work.
intro:
Hostelworld has been selling hostel beds since 1999, and it is one of the very few businesses in budget travel whose numbers you can actually check. Hostelworld Group plc floated on the London Stock Exchange's main market on 2 November 2015 at 185 pence a share, valuing the company at about £176.8 million, and it has published audited accounts ever since. The platform carries roughly 17,000 hostels across more than 180 countries and 13.7 million guest reviews, took 7.0 million net bookings in 2025 on net revenue of €93.8 million, and now sees 63% of its bednights booked through the app rather than the website.

The stay itself is not sold by Hostelworld, and its terms say so in plain words: "your contract for travel services (including accommodation) is with the travel services provider, not Hostelworld". You pay a deposit online — the company's own guide puts it at "about 12-15% of the total cost" — and you settle the balance in person at the hostel, usually alongside a local city tax the property is obliged by law to collect. That split decides who you deal with if anything goes wrong, so it is worth knowing before you book rather than after.

Free cancellation is offered on a large share of properties, and where a hostel sets a standard policy the deadline is, in Hostelworld's words, "normally at least 24 hours before your agreed check-in date". Cancel inside the window and the deposit comes back. There is also a Booking Guarantee for the rare occasion when a reception desk has no record of you, and a best price promise if you find the same bed cheaper elsewhere within a day of booking. Both have conditions attached, and both are set out further down this page.

sections.heading: Where the money goes when you press book
sections.html:
Two of Hostelworld's own documents describe the same payment in different terms, and reading them side by side is the quickest way to understand the business. The consumer booking terms call it "a deposit (being a part payment towards the total value of your booking)". The company's investor presentation is more direct about what it is for: Hostelworld says it will "charge hostels a commission when consumers book on our platform – we collect that commission directly from consumers in the form of a deposit". Both statements are true at once. The money you hand over at the point of booking is the platform's fee, taken from you rather than invoiced to the hostel, and the hostel is paid the rest when you turn up.

That makes the size of the deposit a published figure, because the commission rate is in the accounts. It ran at 15.3% in 2024, 16.2% across 2025, and 17.7% in the six months to 30 June 2026 against 15.8% a year earlier. Set that against a net average booking value of €13.43 in 2025 and €14.90 in the first half of 2026 and the arithmetic is undramatic: on a typical booking the platform keeps something in the region of €14 to €15, and the remainder of the bed price is settled at the hostel counter.

Sitting alongside the deposit is a booking fee. The terms mention it once, to say that "where We charge a booking fee, it is non-refundable in all circumstances", and no amount appears anywhere in the document. That matters more than it first looks, for a reason covered near the end of this page: the booking fee is also the number Hostelworld uses to cap what it can ever owe you.

sections.heading: The balance, the city tax and the costs the search page does not show
sections.html:
Because only the deposit passes through Hostelworld, everything else is a transaction between you and the hostel, and hostels charge for a longer list of things than most hotels do. Hostelworld's own guide to extra costs is unusually candid about it. City or tourist tax is collected "in cash, at check-in or check-out" and hostels are "required by law" to take it: roughly €0.20 to €2 per person per night in France, €1 to €4 in Italy, €0.50 to €4 in Spain, and in the Netherlands around 12.5% of the booking total, which on a week in Amsterdam is a real number rather than loose change.

The rest of the list is smaller but adds up. Bed linen is included almost everywhere; a bath towel is "often extra" at €1 to €3. Lockers can carry a daily fee of €1 to €3 or a refundable deposit on the padlock. Late check-in, where somebody has to stay awake to let you in, runs from €5 to €25. Breakfast is €3 to €6 for a basic spread and €10 or more for a buffet.

A live listing shows how this looks in practice. Castle Hostel 1004 in Bled, rated 9.4 from 2,932 reviews at the time of checking, states a city tax of €3.13 per person per night, luggage storage at €2 per guest and an early or late check-in charge of €5 per person — none of which is in the price you compare on the search results page. Two nights for two people there carries €12.52 of tax alone. Add the extras up before deciding that one hostel is cheaper than another.

sections.heading: Why there is no fourteen-day cooling off on a booked bed
sections.html:
Buy almost anything else online from a UK address and you get 14 days to change your mind. Accommodation is carved out of that right by regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, which excludes services tied to "a specific date or period of performance" — accommodation, transport of goods, vehicle rental, catering and leisure services. A bed booked for the night of the fourteenth is exactly that, so no statutory cancellation right ever attaches to it.

Everything you can cancel, then, you can cancel because a hostel chose to let you, not because the law says so. That is why the cancellation window varies property by property. Hostelworld's terms say deadlines are "normally at least 24 hours before your agreed check-in date, unless otherwise stated", and the Bled listing above sets its own at 72 hours. A non-refundable rate is a different animal again: book one and, in the platform's own words, "you will be charged the full amount of your booking" if you cancel. Simply not turning up is worse still, because the terms let the property charge your card "an amount not exceeding the charge for one night's stay" without asking you first.

The practical reading is that a free cancellation badge is a commercial concession worth checking the exact hours on, and that the discount on a non-refundable rate has to be big enough to be worth losing the whole booking over.

sections.heading: Tours, experiences and the package rule that changes in 2027
sections.html:
A bed on its own is a single travel service. Under regulation 2 of the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 a package needs a combination of at least two different types — carriage of passengers, accommodation, vehicle rental or another tourist service — so accommodation booked alone carries no organiser liability and no insolvency protection. There is no ATOL cover either, because no flight is involved. That is true of every accommodation platform rather than of this one in particular, but it is worth stating plainly: if a hostel closes between your booking and your arrival, nothing in the package travel regime stands behind your deposit.

Hostelworld is more exposed to the next change than a pure bed platform would be, because it also sells tours and experiences alongside accommodation. The Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements (Amendment) Regulations 2026 come into force on 6 April 2027. They delete the linked travel arrangement regime outright, they widen the definition of a package to catch travel services bought under separate contracts where one trader facilitated "the separate selection of and separate payment for each of the travel services" during a single visit to its point of sale, and they replace the old right of redress with a refund obligation running to 14 days. A traveller who books a bed and a walking tour in the same session on the same platform may well be buying a package from April 2027 who is not buying one today.

Nothing on the consumer site addresses this yet, which is unremarkable given the date. It is a reason to check the position again next spring rather than a criticism of the platform now.

sections.heading: What the accounts show about a business built on €15 bookings
sections.html:
The published numbers explain a good deal about how the site behaves. For the year to 31 December 2025, reported on 26 March 2026, net revenue was €93.8 million against €92.0 million, on 7.0 million net bookings. Adjusted EBITDA fell 9% to €19.9 million and the margin slipped from 24% to 21%. Operating profit was €8.4 million and profit for the year €7.0 million. Direct marketing cost €45.3 million, or 48% of generated revenue — close to half of every euro taken. The company still paid a total dividend of 2.40 cent a share and bought back 3.1 million shares for £3.9 million under a £5 million programme, ending the year with €12.2 million of cash and €1.6 million of net debt.

The half-year figures published on 29 July 2026 were stronger. Net revenue rose 12% to €52.2 million on 3.8 million transactions, up just 1%, with the average transaction value up 11% to €14.90. Adjusted EBITDA rose 11% to €8.2 million at a 16% margin, profit for the period was €0.5 million, cash reached €15.0 million and the group moved to €2.5 million of net cash. Marketing absorbed 49% of revenue. Europe produced €26.0 million of the revenue, Asia, Africa and Oceania €16.4 million and the Americas €9.8 million, from a headcount of about 275.

Read those two sets together and the strategy is obvious enough: bookings are barely growing, so revenue growth has to come from taking more per booking. Chief executive Gary Morrison said as much, attributing the half's growth to a tool that "lifted our effective commission rate to 17.7%, up from 15.8% a year earlier". Nobody is hiding it, and a traveller who understands it can shop accordingly.

sections.heading: Reviews written only by people who slept there
sections.html:
The review base is the strongest thing on the platform and it is worth being specific about why. Hostelworld's review guidelines state that "we only accept reviews from customers who have actually booked and stayed at a property booked through our website". A great many travel and retail sites accept reviews from anybody with an account; requiring a completed, verified stay is a meaningfully higher bar, and with 13.7 million reviews collected over more than two decades the sample sizes on individual hostels are large.

Scores are a weighted average across six categories — cleanliness, location, staff, atmosphere, facilities and security — with cleanliness, location and staff carrying more influence than the rest. Hostelworld's own advice on reading them is sensible: treat 50 to 200 reviews as showing "reliable trends emerging", 200 to 1,000 as "strong consistency" and 1,000 or more as "long-term trustworthiness", and "scan the last 10 reviews for the most accurate snapshot", because a hostel under new management can turn in either direction faster than an average will show.

The rules around all of this changed on 7 April 2025, when the consumer protection provisions of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 came into force. Posting or commissioning fake reviews is now explicitly banned, concealed incentivised reviews with it, and the Competition and Markets Authority's guidance of 4 April 2025 requires businesses that publish reviews to take "reasonable and proportionate" steps to detect and deal with them, with any incentive "made apparent". Penalties reach 10% of global turnover. In its first year under those powers the CMA opened investigations into 14 businesses, secured £760,000 of consumer refunds and £4.7 million of fines, issued 157 advisory and warning letters, wrote to 54 firms about reviews and opened five investigations off the back of it. A platform that only accepts reviews from verified stays starts that regime in a comfortable position.

sections.heading: Two guarantees, and the conditions under each
sections.html:
The Booking Guarantee covers the specific nightmare of arriving to find no reservation. If "the property reception agent has no record of your reservation", Hostelworld credits your account with the deposit you paid plus "US$50 extra for the inconvenience caused". Three conditions matter. You must contact the company within 48 hours of arrival through the guarantee form. The money arrives as account credit, not cash, and must be used within 6 months. And it does not apply where a listed property "ceases operation due to unforeseen circumstances" — a hostel that has shut down being, on the face of it, one of the commoner reasons a reception desk cannot find your name.

The best price promise says that "if you find a booking cheaper on any other website, we'll refund you the difference". You have 24 hours from making the booking to claim, and the rival deal must be an exact itinerary match on property, room type, dates and conditions. Blind bookings, membership and loyalty rates, rewards programmes, special promotions and offline group bookings are excluded. The timing is the part to note: the claim "will only be processed after you have checked out of the property and we have verified your stay", with payment by bank transfer within up to 14 days after checkout. You are being reimbursed weeks after the trip, not undercharged at the time.

Neither promise is unusual by the standards of online travel, and having both in writing is better than having neither. They are worth reading as insurance against specific failures rather than as a general assurance.

sections.heading: Elevate, third-party listings and how the results are ordered
sections.html:
The clearest gap between what the company tells investors and what it tells travellers concerns the ordering of search results. In its 2025 results Hostelworld described "the successful launch of ‘Elevate’, our marketplace monetisation tool, which increased our commission rate to 16.7% in H2", and the half-year statement credited Elevate with lifting the rate to 17.7%. What Elevate does mechanically is not explained in either document, and nothing on the consumer site sets out how hostels are ranked, whether a property that pays more appears higher, or how a traveller would tell.

That question has history in this sector. On 13 September 2019 the Competition and Markets Authority concluded action against the accommodation booking industry: 31 firms in total, six of them under formal enforcement — Booking.com, Expedia, Agoda, Hotels.com, ebookers and trivago — on practices including "pressure selling, misleading discount claims and the effect that commission has on how hotels are ordered", together with commitments to stop "giving a false impression of a room's popularity" and to "always display the full cost of a room upfront". Hostelworld was not among the 31 and those undertakings do not bind it. The 2024 Act does bind everybody, and drip pricing — showing one price and adding fees as the customer proceeds — is one of the practices it prohibits.

A second change is worth knowing about for a different reason. In December 2025 Hostelworld launched third-party inventory across 50 destinations and has since extended it to around 18,000, with engagement "strongest on searches with fewer direct Hostelworld results". Some of what a search now returns is accommodation sourced through another supplier rather than a hostel the company deals with directly. That is a reasonable answer to thin results in an unfamiliar city; it does mean the review base and the relationship behind a listing are not uniform across the page, and the site does not label which is which.

sections.heading: Booking from Britain, under Irish law
sections.html:
The corporate structure is more British than the Dublin address suggests, and it is worth a paragraph because it decides who you would be dealing with. The contracting party is Hostelworld.com Limited, registered at 8 Harcourt Street, Dublin 2, D02 AF58, VAT number 9689072B, and the terms are "governed by the laws of Ireland". Above it sits Hostelworld Group plc, company 09818705, incorporated on 9 October 2015 and registered at 1 Chamberlain Square Cs, Birmingham B3 3AX, under SIC code 64209, with accounts last made up to 31 December 2025. A third company in the group carries the history of a rival: Hostelworld Services Limited, company 02841908, was incorporated on 3 August 1993 as MBO MBI Limited, traded as HostelBookers.com Limited from 2 July 2003, and took its present name on 26 May 2015.

Two practical consequences follow. First, the liability cap. Hostelworld's terms limit its "maximum aggregate liability to you" to "the value of the booking fee that has been paid for that booking" — not the deposit, not the room price, the booking fee, which is the one number the terms never put an amount against. Second, there is no ombudsman. Accommodation booking is not a regulated financial service, so the Financial Ombudsman Service has no jurisdiction over it, and no equivalent scheme exists for travel platforms.

If a booking goes badly, the realistic routes are the hostel itself, the Booking Guarantee where it applies, and your card provider. Note one detail before assuming the last of those covers you: section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 bites where the cash price of the item is more than £100 and no more than £30,000, and a deposit of €14 or €15 on a cheap bed sits well below that floor. A chargeback through the card scheme is the more likely mechanism, and the terms on those vary by issuer, so confirm the position with your own bank rather than taking it as read.

pros: Around 17,000 hostels in more than 180 countries, with 13.7 million reviews behind the scores
Reviews come only from people who booked and stayed through the site, which is a stricter test than most travel platforms apply
A small deposit holds the bed; the bulk of the money stays in your pocket until you arrive
Free cancellation is widely available, and the deposit is returned in full inside the hostel's window
Audited, published accounts — you can read the company's revenue, margins and cash position for yourself
The Booking Guarantee pays your deposit back as credit plus US$50 if the hostel has no record of your reservation
Six rated categories per property, weighted towards cleanliness, location and staff
App handles 63% of bednights and shows traveller profiles and chat for the hostel you have booked
cons: The booking fee is never given an amount anywhere in the terms, yet it is non-refundable in every circumstance and is also the ceiling on Hostelworld's liability to you — “limited solely to the value of the booking fee that has been paid for that booking”.

The deposit percentage is not stated in the booking terms either. A company blog post says “about 12-15%” while the group reported an effective commission rate of 17.7% for the first half of 2026, and nothing reconciles the two figures.

Hostels can now pay to improve their position through Elevate, the company's marketplace monetisation tool, and nothing on the consumer site explains how properties are ordered in search results or whether paying more moves one up the page.

Your contract is with the hostel and the terms are governed by Irish law, so a dispute about the stay is not something Hostelworld resolves for you and there is no UK ombudsman scheme covering accommodation bookings.
The best price promise is only paid after you have checked out and the stay has been verified, by bank transfer up to 14 days later — and the claim itself must be made within 24 hours of booking.

The Booking Guarantee pays a site credit rather than cash, it expires after 6 months, and it does not apply where a property “ceases operation due to unforeseen circumstances”, which is one of the likelier ways a booking fails.
The HOSCAR awards are described only as “voted for by YOU”, with no published methodology, no minimum review count and no threshold a hostel must clear to be eligible.
Since December 2025 some results are third-party inventory rather than hostels Hostelworld deals with directly, and the search page does not flag which is which.
verdict: For finding a hostel bed in a city you do not know, Hostelworld is hard to beat: 17,000 properties, 13.7 million reviews written only by people who actually stayed, and a deposit small enough that a change of plan costs you very little. Read it as a directory with a payment system attached rather than as your counterparty, because that is exactly what the terms say it is. Take the free cancellation rate over the non-refundable one unless the discount is large, note the hostel's own deadline rather than assuming 24 hours, and carry enough cash for the balance and the city tax. The things worth grumbling about — an unnamed booking fee that also caps the company's liability, a commission rate climbing from 15.3% to 17.7% in eighteen months, and no published explanation of how the search results are ordered — are worth knowing before you book, not reasons to book somewhere else.

faqs.q: How much does Hostelworld take when I book?
faqs.a: You pay a deposit at the time of booking, which Hostelworld's own guide describes as "about 12-15% of the total cost". The group's accounts put its effective commission rate at 17.7% for the first half of 2026, up from 15.8% a year earlier, on an average booking of €14.90. The rest of the bed price is paid directly to the hostel when you arrive.

faqs.q: Can I cancel and get the deposit back?
faqs.a: Usually, if you are inside the hostel's window. Hostelworld says deadlines are "normally at least 24 hours before your agreed check-in date, unless otherwise stated", and individual properties set their own — 72 hours is common. Non-refundable rates charge the full booking value. There is no statutory 14-day cooling-off period, because regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 excludes accommodation booked for a specific date.

faqs.q: What happens if the hostel has no record of my booking?
faqs.a: The Booking Guarantee credits your account with the deposit plus US$50, provided you contact Hostelworld within 48 hours of arrival and the claim is verified. The credit expires 6 months after it is applied, and the guarantee does not cover a property that has ceased operating.

faqs.q: Are the reviews on Hostelworld reliable?
faqs.a: They are drawn from a narrower pool than most: only customers who booked and stayed through the site may leave one, and there are 13.7 million of them. Scores are a weighted average across cleanliness, location, staff, atmosphere, facilities and security. Read the most recent 10 alongside the headline number, and treat a property with fewer than 50 reviews as unproven.

faqs.q: Do I need anything besides the balance when I arrive?
faqs.a: Bring cash for city tax, which hostels must collect and which is not in the price you compared: roughly €1 to €4 per person per night in Italy, €0.50 to €4 in Spain and around 12.5% of the booking total in the Netherlands. Towels at €1 to €3, lockers at €1 to €3 a day and late check-in at €5 to €25 are common extras.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if something goes wrong with the stay?
faqs.a: The hostel, in the first instance — your contract for the accommodation is with the property, not with Hostelworld, and the platform's terms are governed by Irish law. There is no ombudsman for accommodation bookings, and Hostelworld caps its own liability at the value of the booking fee. A card chargeback is often the practical fallback; section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 will rarely help, because it applies only where the cash price exceeds £100.

title: Insurance2go Phone Insurance Review
meta_title: Insurance2go Phone Insurance: What £1.99 a Month Covers
meta_description: Insurance2go covers phones from £1.99 a month with unlimited claims and 94% accepted in 2024. The excess ladder, the insurers and the claim rules, checked.
intro:
Insurance2go has been selling mobile phone cover since 2007 and is the trading name of Loyal Insurance Services Ltd, a Portsmouth company registered on 2 February 2005 and authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 430316. Since 28 March 2019 it has belonged to SPB, a European affinity insurance group, which runs the brand from 3000 Lakeside, Western Road alongside Better Buy Insurance. Cover starts at £1.99 a month for a phone, and the company says it accepted 94% of the mobile phone claims made in 2024.

The policy is more generous than most network and bank alternatives in one respect that matters: there is no cap on how many times you can claim while it is running. A single premium buys accidental damage, liquid damage, mechanical breakdown, malicious damage, loss and theft, worldwide cover, up to £1,000 of unauthorised calls, texts and downloads in the 24 hours after a theft, £100 against unauthorised e-wallet payments and up to £150 for accessories on any one claim. Claims are assessed within two working days, replacements go out in three to five, and repairs take around five to seven. Buying a year up front costs twelve months for the price of ten, and a second device takes 10% off.

One rule decides whether any of that is open to you. The phone must have been bought in the UK and must be no more than 36 months old on the day the policy starts. Once it is on cover it stays on cover as it ages, but a four-year-old handset cannot be added at all, and neither can one bought overseas or second-hand without a twelve-month warranty from a UK-registered supplier.
