sections.heading: Four covers behind one questionnaire
sections.html:
The tradesman form gathers trade, turnover, staff numbers and work type once, then splits the answers across products that are legally and practically distinct. Public liability answers for injury to a member of the public or damage to their property caused by your work — the drilled pipe, the dropped scaffold board, the customer who trips over a cable run. Employers' liability answers for injury to the people who work for you. They are different obligations with different triggers, and buying one does nothing for the other.

Alongside those, the tradesman pages quote tools and equipment cover, legal expenses, and business buildings and contents for anyone with a yard, workshop or lock-up. A limit of £1 million is the entry point across most of the panel, £2 million and £5 million the common steps above it, and £10 million available on schemes built for larger sites. The number is worth checking against your paperwork before you shop: main contractors, housing associations and local authority frameworks routinely set the limit they will accept, and a quote £40 cheaper at £1m is worthless if the job needs £5m.

What sits behind each result varies. Some marks on the page are insurers writing their own risk; others, Gallagher and Coversure among them, are brokers who will place the risk with an insurer of their choosing. That mix is normal in commercial lines and generally works in a tradesman's favour, because a broker can put an awkward occupation in front of an underwriter who would never appear on a price comparison table. It also means the return time varies: an instant online price and a broker who rings back are both possible outcomes of the same form.

sections.heading: The day a first employee makes cover compulsory
sections.html:
Employers' liability is where the law stops advising and starts requiring. Under the Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969, the Health and Safety Executive's guidance is blunt about the level: “You must be insured for at least £5 million”, though in practice most insurers issue £10 million as standard. Trade without it and you can be fined up to £2,500 for each day you are uninsured. Fail to display the certificate or refuse it to an HSE inspector and that is a further £1,000.

Two details catch out small firms. Since 1 October 2008 there has been no legal duty to keep expired certificates, but the HSE still advises holding them, because industrial disease claims surface decades after exposure and the certificate is what identifies which insurer answers for the year in question. And the exemptions are narrower than the trade talk suggests: a family business where every employee is a close relative is outside the Act, as is a limited company whose only employee owns 50% or more of the share capital, but take on one apprentice from outside the family and the duty starts that morning.

The risk is not theoretical in the building trades. In its latest annual figures the HSE records 126 workers killed in work-related accidents, 59,219 employee injuries reported under RIDDOR, 680,000 people reporting an injury at work in the Labour Force Survey, and 40.1 million working days lost to injury and work-related illness. It puts the annual cost of injury and ill health from current working conditions at £22.9 billion for 2023/24. Construction contributes disproportionately to all of it.

sections.heading: Reading a tools add-on before you need to claim on it
sections.html:
Tools cover is the cheapest line on a tradesman quote and the one most likely to disappoint, because the price is set by conditions the comparison stage never shows you. Take the published terms of one specialist tradesman insurer, Rhino Trade Insurance, as a worked example of the shape: cover from £4.74 a month, or £56.86 for the year, with limits from £500 up to £7,500 and an excess of £100 on each and every claim. Whether that particular scheme appears on the Quotezone panel needs confirming, but the structure is the market's.

The conditions are where the money goes. Overnight cover in a vehicle runs between 10pm and 6am and depends on where the van is parked — a locked garage, your own driveway, or a street in clear view of where you are sleeping. Theft with no sign of forced entry is out. Tools on display in an unlocked vehicle are out. Kit stored anywhere other than the vehicle can be out entirely. Settlement is reduced by 10% depreciation for every year of a tool's age up to a ceiling of 50%, so a five-year-old SDS drill pays out at half its replacement price, and receipts matter because proof of purchase is a condition rather than a courtesy.

One structural point that changes how you shop: on several schemes tools cover is only sold to customers who hold the same insurer's public liability policy. Buying the cheapest liability from one result and the cheapest tools cover from another is not always an option, which makes the combined price the number to compare rather than the headline one.

sections.heading: Belfast, the regulator, and the protections a business does and does not get
sections.html:
Seopa Ltd is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under reference 313860, registered in Northern Ireland as NI46322, and its terms describe its permitted business as “insurance mediation as well as having permission for credit brokerage”, acting as a “non-investment insurance intermediary” and not as a lender. Nothing you buy is a contract with Seopa. The policy, and the promise to pay a claim, belongs to the insurer named on the certificate.

Payment is disclosed plainly: the company “may receive a commission and/or other remuneration from providers, insurers, intermediaries, or other third parties” when you click through, enquire or buy, and its terms invite you to ask for details of what it earns on your particular transaction. Few buyers ever do, and on commercial risks placed through a broker the remuneration can be a meaningful slice of the premium. Whatever is quoted, the standard Insurance Premium Tax rate of 12% is already inside the figure you see.

The part that actually differs for a trade buyer is what happens when something goes wrong. Complaints about the introduction go to Seopa in Belfast, which works to eight weeks before the Financial Ombudsman Service can take over, and a referral must reach the Ombudsman within six months of the final response letter. But a business is only eligible if it is small enough: annual turnover under £6.5 million, fewer than 50 employees or a balance sheet under £5 million, and the complaint must concern an act or omission on or after 1 April 2019. Most sole traders and small firms clear that comfortably. Ombudsman data also shows commercial cases are decided against the firm more often than average: 39% of commercial property complaints and 44% of commercial vehicle complaints were upheld in 2025/26, against 30% across all financial products.

sections.heading: Where the comparison hands the work back to you
sections.html:
No price appears anywhere on the tradesman pages before you complete the form. The site sets out cover levels and legal duties well, then answers the cost question by saying it depends on the trade and the risk profile, which is true and unhelpful in equal measure. There is no indicative premium by trade, no typical excess, and no published list of who is actually on the panel — the 30+ logos are a display, not a roster, and the site quotes panel sizes inconsistently elsewhere.

Professional indemnity is the notable absence from the tradesman line-up. Any trade that specifies, designs or certifies as well as installs — a plumber sizing a heating system, an electrician signing off an installation certificate — carries a professional risk that public liability does not touch. Quotezone sells professional indemnity elsewhere on the site, but it is not part of the tradesman journey, so a buyer who does not already know the distinction will not be prompted to make it.

Support is email only. The company states it does not currently provide a telephone service and aims to reply within two working days, with office hours of 9am to 5pm Monday to Friday. For a trade waiting on a certificate before starting on site, two days is a long time, and the company is clear that any question about the policy itself belongs to the insurer rather than to Quotezone. Your details may also be passed to the providers you are matched with, so expect broker follow-up by phone and email once the form is submitted.

pros: One questionnaire reaches 30+ commercial insurers and brokers, including underwriters who never appear on mainstream price tables
Public liability, employers' liability, tools, legal expenses and business premises cover are gathered in a single journey
Brokers on the panel can place awkward trades - scaffolders, roofers, groundworkers - that direct insurers decline
Free to the user, with commission taken from the provider and disclosed in the terms
Seopa has been FCA-authorised under reference 313860 since 2003 and publishes its address, company number and complaints route
The guidance pages state the legal minimum employers' liability level correctly rather than upselling around it
cons: No indicative price, premium range or typical excess is published for any trade before you hand over your details
Professional indemnity is missing from the tradesman journey, leaving the design and certification risk uncovered for trades that specify as well as install
The 30+ provider marks are logos rather than a published panel list, and panel sizes are stated inconsistently across the site
Support is email only with a two working day reply target and no telephone line, which is slow for anyone needing a certificate before starting on site
Submitting the form passes your details to matched providers, so broker calls and emails follow, and complaints about the policy have to go to the insurer instead
Defaqto publishes star ratings for tradesman insurance, but no independent quality marker appears against results, so cover is sorted on price alone
Commercial buyers sit outside the FCA's consumer pricing rules, which apply only to a person acting outside their trade, business or profession
Tools cover is frequently tied to holding the same insurer's liability policy, so mixing the cheapest result from two providers may not be possible
verdict: As a way of putting one set of trade details in front of 30 or more commercial insurers and brokers at once, Quotezone does the job it claims, and the panel's breadth is the real value for occupations that direct insurers turn away. It is an introduction service, not an adviser: it will not tell you whether £1m or £5m of public liability satisfies your contract, will not flag that a heating designer needs professional indemnity, and will not read the overnight tools condition to you. Check the limit your contract demands, confirm the employers' liability figure the moment you take on staff, and compare the combined liability-plus-tools price rather than the headline. Do that, and the panel earns its keep.

faqs.q: Does Quotezone insure my business itself?
faqs.a: No. Seopa Ltd introduces you to insurers and brokers and is paid commission when you buy. The policy, the claim and the certificate all belong to the provider whose name is on the schedule, and any question about cover goes to them.

faqs.q: How much public liability cover do I actually need?
faqs.a: There is no legal minimum for public liability. In practice the figure is set by whoever hires you: main contractors, housing associations and local authority frameworks commonly specify £5 million, while domestic work is often fine at £1 million or £2 million. Check the contract before comparing, because the cheapest quote at the wrong limit cannot be used.

faqs.q: When does employers' liability become compulsory?
faqs.a: The moment you employ someone who is not exempt. The legal minimum is £5 million, most insurers issue £10 million, and the fine for trading uninsured runs to £2,500 for each day. A further £1,000 applies for failing to produce the certificate when an HSE inspector asks.

faqs.q: Will my tools be covered if they are stolen from the van overnight?
faqs.a: Only if the policy's conditions were met. Schemes typically cover an overnight window such as 10pm to 6am, require the vehicle to be locked and parked somewhere specified, and exclude thefts with no sign of forced entry. Settlement is usually reduced for age, commonly by 10% a year to a maximum of 50%.

faqs.q: Will insurers start phoning me after I fill in the form?
faqs.a: Expect contact. The terms state your information may be passed to the providers you are matched with, and commercial quotes are frequently completed by a broker rather than returned instantly on screen.

faqs.q: What if I have a complaint about the comparison service?
faqs.a: Write to Customer Relations at Seopa Ltd in Belfast or email info@quotezone.co.uk. The firm has eight weeks to give a final response, after which the Financial Ombudsman Service can take the case if you refer it within six months. A business qualifies if turnover is under £6.5 million with fewer than 50 employees or a balance sheet under £5 million.

intro:
Travel insurance is bought in the last ten minutes before a holiday and read for the first time in a hospital corridor. Quotezone puts up to 15 UK travel insurers behind one questionnaire, returns their prices in a few minutes and charges the traveller nothing for it, which at least removes the excuse that shopping around takes too long.

The brand belongs to Seopa Ltd, a Belfast technology firm whose comparison engine has been quoting since the early 2000s; the Quotezone site itself dates its launch to 2005. Seopa now runs over 5 million quotes a year for more than 4 million UK customers across 60+ insurance and finance products, holds relationships with 300+ providers, employs over 70 people across two European offices, and is one of only 11 price comparison services accredited by Ofgem for energy. It has carried Deloitte Best Managed Company status at Platinum level since 2017.

Two figures set the stakes before any price appears. The panel's own published limits run from £10m of emergency medical cover up to unlimited, with cancellation caps between £10,000 and £25,000. And the Association of British Insurers counted £472 million paid out on UK travel claims in 2024. Cover at that scale for the price of a couple of airport pints is the reason the form is worth filling in properly.

sections.heading: The bill a travel policy stands behind
sections.html:
The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office publishes the numbers it has seen British travellers landed with, and they are the most useful thing anyone will read before buying. A broken leg needing hospital treatment in Spain: £25,000 and upwards. Surgery after a quad bike accident in Greece: £80,000. A serious stomach infection in the United States: £150,000.

Insurers met £472 million of UK travel claims across more than 500,000 individual claims in 2024, on ABI figures. Emergency medical treatment took £262 million of that — 34% of the money paid, up from 29% the year before — at an average of £1,528 a medical claim, and one member insurer settled a single case of hospital treatment and repatriation from the USA at over £1 million.

A free UK Global Health Insurance Card is worth carrying and is valid for up to 5 years, but the NHS is blunt that it covers state treatment only. It does not pay for repatriation, treatment in a private facility, or ski and mountain rescue — the three items that turn an incident abroad into a five-figure bill. That gap is what the fifteen insurers on the panel are competing to fill.

sections.heading: Who takes your details, and who pays for the service
sections.html:
Seopa's initial disclosure document is short and unusually candid, and it is the paperwork worth reading before the quotes load. The firm is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority under reference 313860 as a non-investment insurance intermediary and credit broker — a status anyone can confirm on the FCA Register. The document then describes the site as a quote comparison service and internet directory, states plainly that it is not an insurance or financial broker, and adds the sentence that matters most: you will not receive advice or a recommendation from it.

Payment comes from the other side of the transaction. Providers pay Seopa a flat fee, a commission on a completed sale, or a combination, so the traveller pays nothing and the incentive sits with whichever insurers choose to appear. The same document also declines to claim whole-of-market coverage, acknowledging that some insurers stay off comparison sites altogether.

Protection if things go wrong is real but narrow. Seopa aims to answer a complaint by the next working day, and once eight weeks have passed a complainant can take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service. The Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers non-investment insurance mediation at 90% of a claim with no upper limit, rising to 100% for compulsory classes — which travel insurance is not. Note too that every price shown already carries Insurance Premium Tax at the higher rate of 20% rather than the 12% standard rate charged on a car or home policy; travel cover was pulled into the higher band in 1998 and has stayed there.

sections.heading: What the fifteen are quoting on
sections.html:
A single-trip quote generally assumes a holiday of 30 or 31 days; anything longer needs asking for. Annual multi-trip policies typically allow 31 to 45 days per trip, stretch to 90 days on request with some insurers, and cap total time abroad at around 183 days in the year — the trap for anyone splitting a winter between two countries. A family policy usually means two adults living together plus up to 8 children under 18, and pregnancy is commonly covered to 38 weeks.

Where the site earns its keep is showing how far apart the fifteen sit on cover rather than price. Among the specialist medical insurers it lists, AllClear quotes emergency medical to £15m, cancellation to £25,000, baggage to £2,500 and a maximum excess of £500. InsureandGo shows unlimited medical, £10,000 cancellation, £3,000 baggage and a maximum excess of £60. Get Going runs £10m medical with £5,000 of baggage cover, while Freedom and OK To Travel both pair £10m medical with £15,000 cancellation and a £150 excess.

Read that spread twice. Cancellation cover varies by £15,000 between the top and bottom of one short list, and the excess by a factor of more than eight. On a claim for a cancelled family holiday, the difference between a £10,000 cap and a £25,000 cap is worth vastly more than the few pounds separating the premiums. Winter sports, cruise, backpacker and business trips are all quoted through the same form, each adding its own conditions on the cover behind them.

sections.heading: Declaring a condition is where travel cover is won and lost
sections.html:
Every insurer on the panel screens medical history, and the site's own guidance lists the conditions that must be declared even when dormant — arthritis, asthma, cancer in remission, depression, diabetes, epilepsy, heart conditions, high blood pressure, raised cholesterol. Failing to declare one when asked lets the insurer decline the claim. The FCDO gives the same warning about undeclared conditions and pending test results.

Complaint data shows how often this bites. The Financial Ombudsman Service took 4,466 travel insurance complaints in 2023/24, 19% more than the 3,745 of the year before and well clear of the 2,510 it saw in 2019/20, with declined claims over medical conditions said not to have been properly disclosed among the leading causes.

Regulation has already recognised that a standard panel prices serious conditions badly. FCA signposting rules in force since 5 November 2020 require a firm to point a customer towards a directory of specialist medical travel insurers once the medical element of the premium passes a trigger point — set at £100 originally and doubled to £200 from 1 January 2026. The regulator estimated 338,000 to 376,000 consumers a year could benefit, with savings of roughly 40% available to those with more serious conditions who move to a specialist, though its later review found the rules had produced around 21,000 extra policy sales, fewer than expected. The British Insurance Brokers' Association directory those rules point to has now passed 400,000 enquiries. If a quote comes back with a large medical loading, that directory is the next call, not the checkout button.

sections.heading: Where the comparison runs out of road
sections.html:
Fifteen insurers is a thin panel by the standards of the same site's other products, which draw on 300+ provider relationships, and the disclosure document does not pretend otherwise. Several sizeable travel names sell direct only, and a cheapest-on-the-panel price is not a cheapest-in-market price.

No advice means the suitability judgement is entirely the traveller's. On motor cover that is a modest risk; on travel it is the whole game, because the excess, the medical limit and the wording on pre-existing conditions decide whether a claim is paid, and a results page sorted by price puts the £60 excess and the £500 excess side by side with nothing but the premium to tell them apart.

The market itself is under strain, which is worth knowing before renewal. The FCA's value measures data for 2025 shows travel insurance claims costs jumping to 44–48% of premiums from 31–37% in 2024, with premiums up 12% while payouts rose 47%. Claims acceptance across travel products sits at 83–86%, healthier than home insurance, but complaints run at 5–6% of claims, high against other retail insurance lines. Prices are unlikely to fall from here.

Two smaller cautions. Travel to a destination where the FCDO advises against all or all but essential travel will invalidate most policies on the panel, and that is checked at claim stage rather than at purchase. And the initial disclosure document still carries an older Belfast address for Seopa than the one on the site's own about page — a housekeeping detail rather than a regulatory one, but the disclosure document is the piece of paper describing how the firm is paid, so it is the one you would want current.

pros: Up to 15 travel insurers priced from one form, free to the traveller
Single trip, annual multi-trip, backpacker, cruise, winter sports, business and family cover all quoted through the same journey
Publishes side-by-side medical, cancellation, baggage and excess limits rather than price alone
Specialist medical insurers with no upper age limit sit on the panel
FCA-authorised intermediary, reference 313860, with FSCS mediation cover at 90% and no upper limit
Backed by an operation running over 5 million quotes a year for more than 4 million customers
Complaints answered in-house with the Financial Ombudsman Service available after eight weeks
cons: A 15-insurer travel panel is narrow against the 300+ provider relationships the wider site holds, and several travel brands sell direct only
The disclosure document states no advice or recommendation is given, leaving medical limits, excesses and exclusions entirely for the buyer to judge
Results ranked on price put a £60 excess and a £500 excess in the same list, and cancellation caps varying by £15,000 look identical from the outside
Anyone with a serious pre-existing condition may do better through the BIBA medical directory, where the FCA estimates savings of around 40%
Policies on the panel will not respond to travel against FCDO advice, and that is tested at claim stage
The initial disclosure document still shows an older Belfast address than the site's about page
Satisfaction scores shown on the site come from its own review collection rather than an independent audit
verdict: A sensible first stop for a straightforward trip, and genuinely quick: fifteen insurers priced in a few minutes at no cost, with the medical, cancellation, baggage and excess limits laid out where you can see them. Use it as a price benchmark rather than a recommendation, because no advice is given and the panel is not whole of market. Sort on the medical limit and the excess before the premium — a £10,000 cancellation cap against £25,000, or a £500 excess against £60, is worth far more than the pounds between quotes. If you have a serious pre-existing condition and the medical loading comes back over £200, take the signposting seriously and try the specialist directory before buying.

faqs.q: Does Quotezone sell the travel policy itself?
faqs.a: No. It is a quote comparison service and internet directory operated by Seopa Ltd under FCA reference 313860. The contract is with the insurer, and the disclosure document is explicit that no advice or recommendation is given.

faqs.q: How many travel insurers will I see?
faqs.a: Up to 15. That is narrower than the panels behind the site's motor and home products, and it does not claim to be whole of market, so a direct quote from one or two large travel brands is still worth a look.

faqs.q: What does it cost to use?
faqs.a: Nothing to the traveller. Providers pay Seopa a flat fee, a commission on a sale, or a combination of the two.

faqs.q: How long a trip does a policy cover?
faqs.a: Single trip cover is usually written for 30 or 31 days, with longer durations available on request. Annual policies typically allow 31 to 45 days per trip and cap total time abroad at around 183 days in the year.

faqs.q: I have a heart condition — should I use a comparison panel at all?
faqs.a: Get a quote by all means, but declare everything and watch the medical loading. Since 1 January 2026 a firm must point you to a directory of specialist medical travel insurers once that loading reaches £200, and the FCA estimates savings of around 40% for people with more serious conditions who switch to a specialist.

faqs.q: Is a GHIC enough on its own?
faqs.a: No. The card is free and lasts up to 5 years, but it only covers state healthcare. Repatriation, private treatment and mountain rescue are excluded, and the NHS states directly that it is not a replacement for travel insurance.

title: Quotezone.co.uk Van Insurance
meta_title: Quotezone Van Insurance: 60 Providers, £575 Average
meta_description: One form, up to 60 van insurers. The £575 average, the £666.34 saving claim, and the renewal rule that stops short of trade buyers.
intro:
A van is a working asset for most of the people insuring one, and that changes the shape of the buying problem. The premium hangs less on the vehicle than on what you carry in it and who you carry it for, and the underwriters who price a plumber's Transit Custom sensibly are often not the ones advertising at half-time. Quotezone runs up to 60 van insurance providers off a single questionnaire and returns their prices inside a few minutes, free to the person filling it in.

Behind the brand is Seopa Ltd, a Belfast firm trading since 2003 from Blackstaff Studios on Amelia Street, registered in Northern Ireland as NI046322 and authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority that same year under reference 313860. It now processes around 9 million quotes annually across 60+ insurance and finance products, reaches more than 4 million UK customers a year, maintains 300+ provider relationships, and has held Deloitte Best Managed Company status at Platinum level for three consecutive years. The same engine powers CompareNI and the quote forms on partner sites including PistonHeads and TotallyMoney.

Two numbers are worth carrying in with you. Quotezone's own sampling puts the average quoted price for UK van insurance at £575, and its headline claim is that 51% of customers could save £666.34. Both carry conditions, dealt with lower down, but between them they give you a benchmark before the first price lands — and a benchmark is what separates judging a quote from simply accepting one.

sections.heading: Use class is the question that sets your premium
sections.html:
Van pricing turns on a single answer most people give too quickly. Social only covers the van as private transport and nothing else. Social and commuting adds the run to one regular place of work. Carriage of own goods is the class most trades need — your tools, your stock, your materials, moved for your own business. Hire and reward is the different animal: carrying somebody else's goods or property in exchange for payment, which is what parcel and multi-drop delivery work actually is. Haulage sits above that for larger consignments run between depots.

Getting this wrong is not a paperwork error. A carriage-of-own-goods policy will not respond to a claim arising from paid delivery work, and the driver is then uninsured for the purpose — which on a public road carries a £300 fixed penalty and 6 licence points, an unlimited fine and possible disqualification if it reaches court, and the power for police to seize and in some cases destroy the vehicle.

Panel breadth matters more here than it does on a car quote. Several household-name motor insurers decline hire and reward and courier work outright, so a direct enquiry returns nothing at all. Quotezone quotes all six classes through the same form, and for a driver who has just picked up a delivery contract that is the practical value of the service: it finds the specialist schemes without you having to know their names first.

sections.heading: Regional prices, and the cliff at 25
sections.html:
Quotezone publishes its own pricing table rather than a vague range, which is unusual and useful. The national average quoted price is £575. Across twelve UK regions the spread runs from £1,139.81 in London down to £424.83 in South West England — a gap of over £714, meaning a London postcode is quoted at roughly two and a half times a Devon one for otherwise similar risk.

Age moves the number harder than geography does. The average quote for a driver under 25 is £2,026, three and a half times the national figure, and the underlying reason compounds it: a large share of van schemes set a minimum driver age of 25, so a younger driver is not merely quoted more, they are quoted by fewer providers. If you are under 25 and the results screen looks thin, that is why.

The figures rest on a random sample of more than 100,000 UK van policies taken between September and December 2024. That is a real dataset rather than an estimate, and it is also the caveat: it predates the current quoting year, so treat it as a shape rather than a live price. Every one of those figures also has 12% Insurance Premium Tax baked in, the standard rate since 1 June 2017, which is why an insurer's quoted price and its underwriting price are never the same number.

sections.heading: Reading the £666 saving claim properly
sections.html:
The van pages carry a savings figure in two sizes. The page title offers £685; the body text and the buttons say £666. The small print resolves it to a third, more precise number and explains the method: "51% of consumers could save £666.34 on their Van Insurance. The saving was calculated by comparing the cheapest price found with the average of the next five cheapest prices quoted by insurance providers on Seopa Ltd's insurance comparison website." It is dated to April 2026.

Read that method carefully, because it does not say what a quick glance suggests. The comparison is between the cheapest quote on the panel and the average of the next five cheapest quotes on the same panel. It is a measurement of how widely providers disagree with each other, not a measurement of what you would save against your current renewal notice, and not a comparison against the whole market. A driver whose existing insurer happens to be the cheapest on the panel saves nothing at all and the claim remains technically accurate.

Used properly the number is still worth something. A £666.34 gap between first and the average of the next five, on a product averaging £575, tells you the van market disagrees with itself violently — which is the strongest argument there is for running the comparison rather than accepting a renewal. It just is not a discount anyone has promised you.

sections.heading: Tools, goods in transit, and the cover that is not there
sections.html:
The most expensive assumption in van insurance is that the policy covers what is in the back. It does not. A standard van policy excludes tools and equipment carried in the vehicle, goods in transit, wear and tear, mechanical breakdown, and damage caused by cargo that was not properly secured. Each of those is a separate purchase or a separate policy.

Quotezone's form does offer the add-ons: tools and equipment, breakdown cover, a courtesy van, personal injury, medical expenses, legal costs, additional or any-driver cover, windscreen, and European use. The trap is not availability but the conditions attached. Tools cover typically carries a per-item limit as well as an overall one, and almost always an unattended-vehicle clause requiring the van to be locked, alarmed, and frequently emptied overnight. Claims fail on that clause far more often than they fail on the limit.

There is a legislative thread here worth knowing about. The Equipment Theft (Prevention) Act 2023 received Royal Assent on 20 July 2023 and came into force on 20 January 2024. It gives ministers power to restrict the sale of equipment designed for agricultural or commercial use, and of off-road vehicles of at least 250cc or 2kW running on more than two wheels, unless it carries an immobiliser or is "marked with a unique identifier, and a visible indication that it is marked". The Act is live; the regulations that give it teeth still require parliamentary approval, so nothing yet obliges a manufacturer to mark anything. Marking your own kit remains voluntary, and some schemes price it favourably.

sections.heading: A renewal rule that stops short of trade buyers
sections.html:
In 2021 the FCA banned price walking — the practice of quoting a renewing customer more than an equivalent new customer. It reshaped car and home insurance and it is the single biggest reason loyalty stopped paying. The scope is narrower than most people assume. The policy statement is explicit: "Our pricing rules only apply to policies sold to consumers, as defined in our rules. Firms insuring commercial properties or motor fleets will not be subject to the rules for this business."

For a van that distinction is not academic. A van insured privately, in an individual's name for social use, sits inside the protection. A van insured in a company name, or on a commercial basis for trade, may well sit outside it, and a fleet policy certainly does. The practical consequence: if you buy through Quotezone as a business, the rule that quietly polices your renewal price on the family car is not necessarily working on your van. Re-running the comparison every year does that job yourself.

Complaint data points the same way. Across 2025/26 the Financial Ombudsman Service took 214,600 new complaints in total, down sharply from 305,700 the year before. Car and motorcycle insurance produced 13,420 of them with 35% upheld. Commercial vehicle insurance produced far fewer — 1,429 — but they were upheld at 44%, the higher rate of the two. Fewer people complain about van cover, and more of them turn out to have been right.

sections.heading: Belfast, the regulator, and who pays for your quote
sections.html:
Seopa's authorisation under reference 313860 is the right shape for what it does: it introduces you to providers, it does not underwrite. Nothing you buy is a contract with Seopa, and the protection you end up with belongs to the insurer whose name appears on the certificate rather than to the comparison site — a distinction worth holding onto, because Financial Services Compensation Scheme cover attaches to the insurer, and motor insurance sits in the compulsory class that carries the fullest protection.

On money, the company is direct. Its explanation of revenue states that "if you buy insurance from one of our partners through the Quotezone website, this is when we make money", taken "as either a flat fee or a commission payment depending on the insurance product". It also states that "the results we provide to our customers are not affected by any fees we receive from providers". Payment lands on a completed sale, not a click, which at least aligns the incentive with quoting you something you actually want.

One absence is worth flagging. Defaqto rates commercial vehicle insurance, assessing between 30 and 100 features per policy and reducing them to a 1 to 5 star score. Those ratings do not appear against Quotezone's van results. On a product where the difference between two similarly priced policies is the tools limit, the excess, and the unattended-vehicle wording, an independent quality marker alongside the price would tell you more than the price does. Its absence means the sorting you get is by cost alone.

If the introduction itself goes wrong, complaints go to Seopa in Belfast first, and to the Financial Ombudsman Service after eight weeks. Complaints about the policy go to the insurer, not to Quotezone.

pros: Up to 60 van providers from one questionnaire, free to use, with no charge added to the premium you are quoted
Quotes all six use classes including hire and reward, courier and haulage, which several large direct insurers decline outright
Publishes its own pricing data - a £575 national average and a twelve-region table - rather than an unsourced range
FCA authorised under reference 313860 since 2003, run by a Belfast company trading for over twenty years
Add-ons for tools, goods handling, breakdown, legal costs and European use are quoted in the same pass
Clear published statement that provider fees do not affect the results shown
cons: The £666.34 saving compares the cheapest panel quote with the average of the next five cheapest on the same panel - it measures disagreement between providers, not a saving against your current renewal
The van page itself carries two different savings figures, £685 in the title and £666 in the body, before the small print resolves it to £666.34
Business and commercial van policies sit outside the FCA's consumer renewal-pricing rules, so the ban on charging renewing customers more than new ones may not protect a trade buyer
The £575 average and the regional table are built on policies sampled between September and December 2024, so the benchmark is well over a year old
No Defaqto star rating appears alongside results, despite Defaqto rating commercial vehicle insurance, so policies are sorted on price rather than on what the cover contains
Panel size is stated inconsistently across the site - up to 60 on the van pages, 50+ on the revenue explanation - and no list of who is actually on it is published
Not whole of market and no advice is given, so the choice of excess, tools limit and use class rests entirely with you
Many van schemes set a minimum driver age of 25, and the £2,026 average for under-25s reflects a thinner panel as well as a higher risk
Tools and goods in transit are excluded from every standard policy and sold as add-ons whose unattended-vehicle conditions the comparison does not surface
Satisfaction scores differ by page - 4.88 out of 5 from 172 reviews on the van section against 4.71 from 3,349 across the site - and both are self-reported rather than independently audited
verdict: For anyone whose van does anything more complicated than sit on a driveway, this is a sensible first stop rather than a last word. The panel's real value is reach into hire and reward, courier and haulage work, where the familiar direct insurers simply refuse to quote and a specialist scheme is the only answer. The published pricing - £575 average, £2,026 under 25, £1,139.81 in London against £424.83 in the South West - gives you something to judge the results against, which most comparison sites decline to provide. Treat the £666.34 headline as evidence that the market disagrees with itself rather than as a promise, ignore the ordering of the results long enough to compare the tools limit and the unattended-vehicle wording on the two or three cheapest, and if the van is insured for trade, diarise the comparison for next year - because the renewal rule that protects your car may not reach it.

faqs.q: Does Quotezone insure the van itself?
faqs.a: No. Seopa Ltd is an introducer, authorised by the FCA under reference 313860. The contract, the certificate, the claim and the complaint all belong to whichever provider you buy from. Quotezone is paid a flat fee or a commission by that provider when a sale completes.

faqs.q: What is the difference between carriage of own goods and hire and reward?
faqs.a: Carriage of own goods covers your own tools, stock and materials moved for your own business. Hire and reward covers carrying someone else's goods for payment - parcel delivery, multi-drop and courier work. A carriage-of-own-goods policy will not respond to a claim arising from paid delivery work, which leaves you uninsured for that use: a £300 fixed penalty and 6 points, an unlimited fine at court, and possible seizure of the vehicle.

faqs.q: Are my tools covered by a van policy?
faqs.a: Not as standard. Tools and equipment in the vehicle, and goods in transit, are excluded from every standard van policy and sold as add-ons. Where you buy the add-on, check the per-item limit as well as the overall limit, and read the unattended-vehicle condition - most require the van locked and alarmed, and many require tools removed overnight.

faqs.q: Is £575 what I should expect to pay?
faqs.a: It is the average quoted price from a random sample of more than 100,000 UK van policies taken between September and December 2024, so treat it as a shape rather than a live price. Your own figure moves on postcode - £1,139.81 average in London against £424.83 in South West England - on age, with under-25s averaging £2,026, and on use class. Insurance Premium Tax at 12% is already inside all of those numbers.

faqs.q: Will comparing every year still save money on a business van?
faqs.a: More than it does on a private car, if anything. The FCA's ban on charging renewing customers more than equivalent new customers applies only to policies sold to consumers - the policy statement says firms insuring commercial properties or motor fleets are not subject to it. A van held on a commercial basis may sit outside that protection, so the annual comparison is the only thing doing that job.

title: Row.co.uk Phone Insurance Review
meta_title: Row.co.uk Phone Insurance: Cover From £1.49 a Month
meta_description: Row.co.uk covers phones and gadgets from £1.49 a month, underwritten by Collinson. We check the tiered excess, the 12-month age limit and how claims are paid.
intro:
Row.co.uk sells mobile phone and gadget cover from £1.49 a month, or £1.41 a month if you pay for the year up front, and it has built its name on breadth. One policy can wrap a phone, a laptop, a camera, a games console and more, and the price drops by 5% for every extra device you add, up to 15% off, or 20% on an annual plan. Behind the low headline sits a substantial insurer: the cover is carried by Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited (firm reference 202846), which wrote £297.2 million of premium in its 2025 financial year.

The day-to-day brand is run by BIG Warranties Limited, a Poole company authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority under reference 798998, and the phone cover is fuller than the add-ons a network or a bank tends to sell. It pays for cracked screens, liquid damage, accidental damage, mechanical breakdown, and theft, loss and unauthorised calls, and it travels with you across the UK and for up to 90 days abroad in any year. A gadget is also covered while it is in the hands of an immediate family member, Row aims to get a replacement to your door within 24 hours of approving a claim, and accidental-damage claims are unlimited across a policy year.

key_facts.label: Administrator and brand
key_facts.value: BIG Warranties Limited (company 07002567), FRN 798998, Poole

key_facts.label: Insurer carrying the risk
key_facts.value: Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited (company 01708613), FRN 202846

key_facts.value: £1.49 a month, or £1.41 a month paid annually

key_facts.value: 5% per extra device, up to 15% off (20% on an annual plan)

key_facts.label: Standard excess
key_facts.value: £40 if the gadget is covered for £200 or less, £75 above that, £80 for a laptop

key_facts.label: Additional excess
key_facts.value: £30 more for each of loss or theft, an international claim, and a claim in the first three months

key_facts.value: £100 per claim

key_facts.value: Up to £1,000 including VAT, for 48 hours after a valid theft claim

key_facts.value: Up to 90 days outside the UK in any one year

key_facts.value: Under 12 months old at the date of application

key_facts.value: No claim paid in the first 14 days of the policy

key_facts.value: Unlimited accidental damage and breakdown; one theft or loss claim per policy year

key_facts.value: New or reconditioned units

key_facts.label: Cancellation
key_facts.value: 14-day statutory right; annual policies refunded pro rata less a £30 administration charge; no refund once a claim is made

key_facts.label: Independent rating
key_facts.value: Smart Money People 4.51 out of 5 from 247 reviews, last reviewed 31 March 2019

sections.heading: Who carries the risk, and who you deal with
sections.html:
Two firms stand behind a Row.co.uk policy. BIG Warranties Limited is the administrator: it takes your money, answers the phone and handles the claim, and it holds firm reference 798998 on the FCA register. The insurer that actually pays is Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited (company 01708613, firm reference 202846), part of the Collinson group. Astrenska is not a minor name. Its 2025 solvency report shows gross written premium of £297.2 million, up from £221.4 million the year before, a profit after tax of £4.3 million, and a solvency coverage ratio of 176%, down from 205%. Its book expressly includes “Property Ancillary, Mobile, Gadget and Cycle Insurance products”, so phone cover is core to what it does rather than a sideline.

BIG Warranties itself is worth a moment. Companies House shows it was incorporated on 27 August 2009 as Elite Sky Repairs Limited and took its present name on 10 November 2010, a repair business that grew into a warranty and insurance administrator. Row.co.uk is now one shopfront on a wider range that runs to appliance cover, boiler and home-emergency plans, motor breakdown and even a novelty “Pokédex” gadget policy, all sold from the same Poole office.

sections.heading: Where the £1.49 earns its money back
sections.html:
The premium is genuinely low, so the excess is the figure to read before you buy. Row publishes it plainly, which many rivals do not: £40 where a gadget is covered for £200 or less, £75 where it is covered for more, and £80 for a laptop. On top of that the wording adds a further charge, and this is the part that repays close reading. It states that “an additional £30 excess will be applied for each of the following: loss or theft, international claims, claims within the first three months of the policy start date”. Because those add up, a phone insured for more than £200 that is lost while you are abroad in the second month of cover carries £75 plus three separate £30 charges, a £165 excess before the policy pays a penny; a laptop in the same situation reaches £170. The events that trigger the surcharges, theft, loss and travel, are the ones most people buy the cover for.

Two smaller limits are worth knowing. Accessories are capped at £100 a claim, whatever the phone is worth, and cover for unauthorised calls after a theft runs for only 48 hours from the theft, to a ceiling of £1,000 including VAT.

sections.heading: The rules on what you can insure
sections.html:
Row will only start cover on a device that is under 12 months old at the date of application. That is a narrower door than several phone specialists, which accept handsets up to two or three years old, and it shuts out precisely the ageing phones whose batteries and screens are most likely to fail. Once you are on cover, nothing is paid for a claim in the first 14 days, accidental-damage and breakdown claims are unlimited, but you may claim only once for theft or loss in a policy year.

The family clause is narrower than it first appears. A gadget is covered in an immediate family member’s hands for breakdown and accidental damage, but not for theft or loss, so a phone lent to a partner and then stolen would fall outside that extension. Replacements “may be new or reconditioned units”, so an approved claim will not always return a brand-new handset. Cancelling inside 14 days brings a refund, but an annual policy cancelled later is refunded pro rata less a £30 administration charge, and there is no refund at all once a claim has been made.

sections.heading: The gadget market in the regulator’s numbers
sections.html: There is useful context in the FCA’s general insurance value measures data for 2025, published on 21 July 2026. Across the whole market, the share of gadget premiums paid back out in claims fell from 42% to 36%, one of the steepest drops of any product line, with 7.5 million gadget policies in force after a 5% fall in the year. The figure is about the market, not about Row, and it cuts both ways: cover is getting cheaper to run, which is good for insurers’ margins and less obviously good for buyers. What the release does not give for gadget cover is a claims-acceptance rate, the way it does for motor and home, and the Financial Ombudsman Service does not break out a gadget or mobile-phone uphold rate either, so there is no published benchmark to hold Row’s claims record against. That absence is a fact about the whole product, and worth knowing before you assume any gadget policy is a safe bet.

sections.heading: How much independent evidence there is
sections.html: Row is not rated by Defaqto for gadget cover, and no Which? or Fairer Finance assessment of the product could be found, which is common for this corner of the market but leaves little to lean on. The one independent source that carries it, Smart Money People, scores Row.co.uk gadget insurance 4.51 out of 5, but from 247 reviews last refreshed on 31 March 2019, so the number reflects a policy sold more than seven years ago rather than the cover on offer today. A recent, dated rating would tell a buyer far more, and none exists.

pros: Among the cheapest headline prices on the market, from £1.49 a month, or £1.41 paid annually
One policy can cover several gadgets, with 5% off per extra device up to 15% (20% on an annual plan)
Backed by a sizeable insurer, Astrenska Insurance Limited, which wrote £297.2 million of premium in 2025
Unlimited accidental-damage and breakdown claims across a policy year
Up to 90 days of cover abroad and a replacement aimed within 24 hours of a claim being approved
The standard excess is published on the site, which is more than many phone insurers do
cons: The £30 additional excesses stack: a phone covered for over £200 that is lost abroad in the first three months carries a £165 excess (£170 for a laptop) before the policy pays anything
Cover can only start on a device under 12 months old, shutting out the older phones most likely to need it
No claim is paid in the first 14 days of the policy, and only one theft or loss claim is allowed per year
The family extension covers breakdown and accidental damage only, not theft or loss, and replacements may be reconditioned rather than new
An annual policy cancelled after 14 days is refunded less a £30 administration charge, with no refund at all once a claim has been made
The only independent rating, Smart Money People’s 4.51 from 247 reviews, was last reviewed on 31 March 2019, and there is no Defaqto or Which? assessment
verdict: Row.co.uk is a cheap, broad gadget policy from a small Poole administrator, sitting on the balance sheet of a real insurer in Astrenska. The headline of £1.49 a month is honest as far as it goes, and the multi-gadget discount makes it attractive if you want one policy over several devices. The catch is the excess: the £30 surcharges for theft, loss and travel stack, so the exact claims most people insure against can cost £165 or more before anything is paid, and the 12-month age limit rules the policy out for older handsets. Read the excess table and check your phone’s age before you judge it on price alone.

faqs.q: Who underwrites Row.co.uk phone insurance?
faqs.a: The policy is administered by BIG Warranties Limited (firm reference 798998) and underwritten by Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited (company 01708613, firm reference 202846), part of the Collinson group. Astrenska wrote £297.2 million of premium in its 2025 financial year.

faqs.q: What would the excess be if my phone were lost abroad?
faqs.a: For a phone insured for more than £200, the standard excess is £75. The wording adds £30 for a loss or theft claim, £30 for an international claim, and £30 for a claim in the first three months, and these apply separately. A phone lost abroad in the first three months would therefore carry a £165 excess; a laptop, £170.

faqs.q: Can I insure an older phone with Row.co.uk?
faqs.a: No. Cover can only start on a device that is under 12 months old at the date of application. Several phone specialists accept handsets up to two or three years old, so if your phone is older you would need a different provider.

faqs.q: Is my family covered under my policy?
faqs.a: A gadget is covered while in the possession of an immediate family member, but only for breakdown and accidental damage. Theft or loss while the device is with a family member is not covered by that extension.

faqs.q: How quickly is a claim settled?
faqs.a: Row aims to get a replacement to your door within 24 hours of approving a claim, or to complete a repair within about three working days. Replacements may be new or reconditioned units, and there is a 14-day exclusion period at the start of the policy during which no claim is paid.

title: Saga Landlord Insurance Review
meta_title: Saga Landlord Insurance: £1m Cover, Arranged by Uinsure
meta_description: Saga landlord insurance gives £1m buildings and £2m liability cover, arranged through Uinsure since October 2024. Limits, fees and conditions checked.
intro:
Saga has been selling to people over 50 since 1951, and insurance has been the steady half of the business for most of that time. The group finished its financial year on 31 January 2026 with 1,294,000 insurance policies on the books, a customer database of 9.3 million people and underlying revenue of £654.6m, up 11% on the year before. Landlord cover is a small corner of that, but it is a well-built one: buildings protection up to £1,000,000, contents up to £35,000, property owners liability of £2,000,000, and a product that has held a Defaqto 5 Star rating every year since 2015.

The policy you buy from Saga today is arranged and run by Uinsure Limited, a Manchester firm Saga partnered with on 1 October 2024. Saga puts its name and its over-50s audience to the product; Uinsure sets the price, picks the insurer from its panel and handles the claim. That is worth knowing before you ring, because it decides which phone number you need and whose complaints department you would be writing to.

key_facts.label: Arranged by
key_facts.value: Uinsure Limited (FRN 463689) since 1 October 2024

key_facts.label: Sold by
key_facts.value: Saga Services Limited (FRN 311557)

key_facts.label: Buildings cover
key_facts.value: Up to £1,000,000, or rebuild cost for a flat

key_facts.label: Loss of rent / alternative accommodation
key_facts.value: 20% of the buildings claim limit

key_facts.label: Rent guarantee (optional)
key_facts.value: £2,500 a month for up to 12 months

key_facts.label: Home emergency (optional)
key_facts.value: £1,000 per claim, unlimited claims

key_facts.label: Unoccupancy limit
key_facts.value: 60 consecutive days

key_facts.label: Defaqto
key_facts.value: 5 Star landlord rating since 2015

sections.heading: One date in October split this policy in two
sections.html:
Saga landlord policies sold on or before 30 September 2024 were underwritten by Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance plc, company number 93792, on a Saga-branded wording. Everything sold from 1 October 2024 comes through Uinsure Limited instead — company number 06046870, registered at the XYZ Building, Hardman Boulevard, Manchester M3 3AQ, and authorised by the FCA under firm reference 463689, a number you can check yourself on the Financial Services Register.

Saga keeps both routes open and staffs them separately. An older RSA-era policy is serviced on 0800 027 1355 from 9am to 5.30pm on weekdays, with a claims line on 0800 027 1357 that runs around the clock. A policy bought since the changeover goes to Uinsure on 0344 844 3844, weekdays 9am to 5pm, and the Saga-badged sales team at Uinsure answers 0161 524 3051 from 8.30am to 7pm on weekdays and 9am to 3pm on Saturdays. Ring the wrong one and you will be transferred rather than helped.

The split matters for a second reason. Saga sold its own underwriter, Acromas Insurance Company Limited, to Ageas for £65m plus £2.5m on completion, and signed a 20-year partnership worth £80m upfront and up to £30m in contingent payments. Motor went live under that arrangement in December 2025 and home followed on 23 April 2026. Landlord did not go to Ageas. It went to Uinsure seven months before the Ageas deal was even announced, and it sits outside the partnership that now defines the rest of Saga's insurance business.

sections.heading: What the £1m headline actually buys
sections.html:
The buildings limit is £1,000,000, or the rebuild cost if the property is a flat. Underneath it sit the sub-limits that decide most real claims. Trace and access — the cost of pulling up a floor to find a leak — is covered to £10,000, which is generous; a great many landlord policies stop at £5,000. Replacing locks after keys are lost or stolen is covered to £1,000. Metered water and oil lost through an escape is covered to £1,500. Theft from outbuildings, on the contents section, is limited to £1,000.

Liability is where the numbers get large. Property owners liability runs to £2,000,000 and liability to a domestic employee — a cleaner or a gardener you pay — to £5,000,000. Both are the market standard rather than a selling point, but a landlord without the second one is exposed in a way that is easy to overlook.

Loss of rent and the cost of rehousing a tenant are treated as one pot, capped at 20% of the buildings claim limit. On a £250,000 rebuild figure that is £50,000, which is ample. Buy contents cover on its own and the equivalent pot is £3,000 at the £15,000 contents level or £7,000 at £35,000 — a much tighter number, and the one that applies if you let a flat where the freeholder insures the structure.

Set those against what the market is actually paying out. The ABI's property tracker put £846m of home claims settled in the first quarter of 2026, an average claim of £6,340 against an average combined premium of £375, and by the second quarter the average subsidence claim had reached a record £20,000. A £10,000 trace and access limit stops looking like small print at that point.

sections.heading: The optional covers are where the conditions live
sections.html:
Legal expenses and rent guarantee are provided through Arc Legal Assistance Limited, FCA firm reference 305958, and they are the parts of the policy most likely to be bought and least likely to be read. Legal cover runs to £100,000 with unlimited access to the advice line, extends to £1,000,000 for a Defective Premises Act claim, and pays £20,000 if a tax liability falls due on accidental death. A tax dispute carries a £200 excess.

Rent guarantee pays £2,500 a month for a maximum of twelve months. The excess is one month's rent, arrears below £250 are outside the cover, and Arc will not run a case it rates at less than a 51% chance of winning. It also requires the tenant referencing paperwork to exist — a claim without it is declined on the file rather than on the merits.

That condition has become sharper since 1 May 2026, when the Renters' Rights Act 2025 converted most existing assured shorthold tenancies into assured periodic tenancies and removed Section 21 altogether. Possession now runs through Section 8 grounds, which takes longer, and a Section 8 notice served since commencement stays live for twelve months rather than the six a Section 21 notice used to give. Landlords also had to issue tenants an information sheet by 31 May 2026, with penalties reaching £7,000 for not doing it. Twelve months of rent guarantee is a different proposition when possession itself has slowed down.

Home emergency is the third add-on: £1,000 including VAT per claim, with no cap on the number of claims in a year. It carries a 48-hour waiting period from inception unless you held equivalent cover immediately before, and you must report a problem within 48 hours of noticing it.

sections.heading: Fees, excesses and the things the quote does not show you
sections.html:
Uinsure's own terms of business document, in its September 2025 version, sets an annual administration fee of £48 on landlord insurance and £36 on home insurance, on top of the premium and the insurer's commission. Instalment charges are levied separately by Close Brothers. None of that appears on Saga's landlord pages, so treat £48 as the figure to look for on the quote summary and confirm it before you pay.

Excesses are harder to pin down, because the wording defers all of them to the schedule you are shown at quote. There is no published standard excess, no published escape of water excess and no published subsidence excess anywhere in the customer-facing documents — and subsidence is the one that hurts, given the £20,000 average claim now being recorded. You cannot compare this policy on excess until you have run a quote, which is a real obstacle to shopping around and needs confirming case by case.

The security condition is published, and it has teeth. Uinsure's landlord wording requires the final exit door and any other external, sliding, patio or double-leaf french doors to carry a five-lever mortise deadlock conforming to BS3621, a rim automatic deadlock or a multi-point locking system. An older let with original door furniture may not meet that, and the time to find out is before a theft claim rather than after one.

One more piece of housekeeping. The FCA has a standing warning about a clone firm using the Saga Services name, first published on 17 August 2020 and last updated on 29 March 2021, which was operating on 0208 002 8791. The genuine firm is Saga Services Limited, FRN 311557, at 3 Pancras Square, London N1C 4AG. If a Saga landlord quote arrives from a number you did not dial, check it against the Register before sending money.

sections.heading: Sixty empty days, and the sixty-first
sections.html:
Cover under several sections falls away once the property has been unoccupied for more than 60 consecutive days. That is a fairly standard allowance and slightly better than the 30 days some landlord wordings impose, but the count is of consecutive days with nobody living there, not days between tenancies on paper. A void running from a tenant leaving in early July to a new one moving in mid-September crosses it.

Optional malicious damage cover is the add-on landlords most often want, and it is also the one the unoccupancy rule bites hardest. Damage by a tenant, their staff or their guests is excluded from the standard policy unless the extension is bought, and drug cultivation damage sits behind the same extension. Neither responds while the property is over the 60-day line.

Saga's own home book gives some sense of how the market has moved. Home policies in force fell 19% over the year to 31 January 2026, from 506,000 to 412,000, while motor rose 12% to 675,000 — the shape of a business that has been repricing property risk hard. The Financial Ombudsman Service, in the annual figures it published on 21 May 2026, logged 6,399 new buildings insurance complaints against 214,600 across all products, with an average uphold rate of 30%. Property claims are argued about more than most, and the wording is where those arguments get settled.

pros: Buildings cover to £1,000,000, or full rebuild cost on a flat, with £2,000,000 property owners liability and £5,000,000 for domestic employees
Trace and access to £10,000, which is double the limit many landlord policies stop at
Loss of rent and rehousing pooled at 20% of the buildings claim limit rather than a flat cash cap
Defaqto 5 Star rated landlord product every year since 2015, and home since 2014
Two staffed service routes kept open, so pre-October 2024 RSA policies still have a 24-hour claims line
Rent guarantee at £2,500 a month for a full twelve months, with unlimited legal advice included
cons: The £48 annual administration fee in Uinsure's terms of business is not mentioned anywhere on Saga's landlord pages, so it only surfaces at quote
No excess figures are published at all — standard, escape of water and subsidence all defer to the schedule, which makes the policy impossible to compare before quoting
Cover under several sections stops after 60 consecutive days of the property being empty, and that includes the optional malicious damage extension landlords buy specifically for void periods
Malicious damage by a tenant and drug cultivation damage are both excluded unless you pay for the extension
Home emergency will not respond on a boiler over 15 years old or rated above 238,000 btu, or on a flat roof over 10 years old — common features of older let property
Rent guarantee needs tenant referencing on file and a 51% prospect of success before Arc Legal will act, and arrears under £250 are outside it entirely
The Saga brand is doing the marketing while Uinsure sets the price, holds the panel and answers the phone, so a Saga quote is a Uinsure quote in Saga livery
verdict: A capable landlord policy sold under a brand that no longer builds it. The limits are sound — £1,000,000 buildings, £2,000,000 liability, £10,000 trace and access, twelve months of rent guarantee at £2,500 — and the Defaqto rating has held since 2015. What you are buying is Uinsure's panel product with Saga's name on the front, priced by Uinsure and claimed against with Uinsure, and the two things to settle before you commit are the £48 administration fee and the excesses, neither of which is published. If your property sits empty between tenancies for long stretches, read the 60-day condition first.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites Saga landlord insurance?
faqs.a: Since 1 October 2024 the policy is arranged by Uinsure Limited (FRN 463689), which places the risk with an insurer from its own panel. The individual insurer is named on your policy schedule rather than on Saga's website. Policies bought on or before 30 September 2024 were underwritten by Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance plc.

faqs.q: Do I have to be over 50 to buy it?
faqs.a: Saga markets the product to the over-50s and none of its landlord pages states a hard minimum age. Because the quote is produced by Uinsure rather than Saga, eligibility is set on Uinsure's system, so confirm it on the quote if you are under 50 rather than assuming either way.

faqs.q: How long can the property be empty?
faqs.a: Sixty consecutive days. Past that, cover under several sections — including the optional malicious damage extension — stops until the property is lived in again. Tell Uinsure before a longer void starts rather than after it.

faqs.q: What does the rent guarantee cover pay?
faqs.a: Up to £2,500 a month for a maximum of twelve months, with an excess equal to one month's rent. Arrears below £250 are excluded, tenant referencing must be on file, and Arc Legal Assistance (FRN 305958) will only run a case it rates at 51% or better.

faqs.q: Is there a fee on top of the premium?
faqs.a: Uinsure's September 2025 terms of business set a £48 annual administration fee on landlord policies, with instalment charges applied separately by Close Brothers. Saga's own pages do not mention it, so check the quote summary before paying.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: For a policy bought since October 2024, Uinsure Customer Services at PO Box 1189, Doncaster DN1 9RP, or 0330 912 2502. If eight weeks pass without resolution you can take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which upheld 30% of the 214,600 complaints it closed in the year to 31 March 2026.

title: Simply Business Tradesman Insurance Review
meta_title: Simply Business Tradesman Insurance: What It Costs
meta_description: Simply Business quotes tradesman cover from £5.40 a month across a panel of 19 insurers. The prices, the limits, the excesses and the fees, checked.
intro:
Simply Business started in 2005 as a team of five people trying to sell business insurance online at a time when almost nobody did. It now covers more than one million small businesses and landlords across roughly 1,500 trades, employs over 900 people from offices in London and Northampton, and paid out £57 million in claims during 2025 — an average of about £156,000 a day. On the tradesman side alone it puts the figure at more than 253,000 tradespeople on cover. Quotes start at £5.40 a month and the site reckons on about seven minutes to complete one.

It does not carry the risk itself. Simply Business is the trading name of Xbridge Limited, an insurance broker, and the policy you end up with is written by one of the insurers on its panel — AXA, Aviva, Zurich, Allianz, QBE, Covéa, Hiscox, Markel, Churchill or AIG among them. That is a point in its favour rather than against it: a sole trader paying £7 a month is getting paper from companies that would not normally quote a one-person business directly. The whole operation has been owned by the American insurer Travelers since 2017, which bought it from Aquiline Capital Partners for around $490 million when it had 425,000 customers and had placed £93 million of premium in 2016.

What follows is what the cover actually contains, what the excesses look like on the two wordings the site publishes openly, what paying monthly adds, and where the paperwork runs out.
